screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: First We Bombed New Mexico - the Aftermath
screenings.description: The inspiring story of a relentless Latina cancer survivor who takes on 80 years of injustice by the U.S. government. Tina Cordova catalyzes a movement to secure acknowledgement and compensation for the ignored Native American and Hispanic cancer victims of the Trinity Bomb’s radioactive fallout. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH exposes the racism and nuclear colonization that enabled New Mexico to become America’s nuclear bomb–making state. The film screens during a moment of grave global insecurity. This film personalizes the unthinkable human cost of another nuclear incident. An earlier version of the film won 16 festival awards, including Best Director and Best Documentary at the Paris Cine Film Festival, Best Documentary Feature and Best Directing at the Worldwide Women’s Film Festival, and the Jury Prize for Best Historical Documentary at the San Antonio Film Festival. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH reveals an unknown story that has captured audiences. The film was a part of the momentum that led to Congress awarding compensation to New Mexico Downwinder families in 2025. The inspirational re-release witnesses a people who were once considered powerless and voiceless finally gaining recognition after years of fighting for justice.

screenings.title: Miss Representation: Rise Up
screenings.description: Over a decade after MISS REPRESENTATION exposed the media’s contribution to the underrepresentation of women in leadership, this follow-up dives deep into the cultural backlash against women’s agency and power. With the proliferation of AI and deepfakes, a new era of tech-facilitated violence is exacerbating sexism and misogyny in an attempt to control and silence women and girls. With inspiring young women at its core, MISS REPRESENTATION: RISE UP interweaves their personal journeys with powerful voices in media, culture, leadership, and academia to reimagine a future that finally uplifts women and girls.

screenings.title: Ralph Bunche: an American Odyssey
screenings.description: U.S., 2001 Directed by William Greaves Screenplay by William Greaves Based on the biography by Brian Urquhart Narrated by Sidney Poitier Approx. 116 min. The first in-depth documentary film about Dr. Ralph Johnson Bunche (1903-1971): statesman, peace negotiator, leading intellectual, and scholar, who rose to the position of Under-Secretary General of the U.N. and was the first person of color to win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1950. Presented with support from The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film Presented with support from The Richard Brick, Geri Ashur, and Sara Bershtel Fund for Social Justice Documentaries

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire

screenings.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
screenings.description: Harry is an old-school hustler. A classic native New Yorker, he moves through life lubricating palms with cash, relying on his wits and connections. But times are changing for Harry. His daily pickpocket take isn’t green bills and wristwatches, it’s credit cards and cell phones. And one unfortunate night, cryptocurrency and a handgun. THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

screenings.title: Wicker
screenings.description: On the outskirts of a village by the sea, lives a Fisherwoman; smelly, single and perpetually ridiculed. One day, fed up with her stuffy, small-minded neighbors, she commissions herself a husband to be made from wicker. In an otherwise conservative town, this unconventional romance sparks outrage, jealousy and chaos.

screenings.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
screenings.description: From writer-director Bassam Tariq, YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devoutly religious hitman who struggles to balance work, faith and fatherhood. When his wife dies, he embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children, confronting the forces closing in around him - and the beliefs threatening to unravel within.

screenings.title: The History of Concrete
screenings.description: Following the finale of his TV show, filmmaker John Wilson searches for a new creative outlet. After attending a workshop on how to write and sell a Hallmark movie, he attempts to apply the same formula to a documentary about concrete.

screenings.title: La Bola Negra
screenings.description: From Cannes-winning directors Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi — popularly known as Los Javis —LA BOLA NEGRA follows three generations of men across pivotal moments in Spanish history, bound by pain, desire, and love. Carlos (Milo Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And Alberto (Carlos González) uncovers a long-buried family secret — one that finally gives voice to truths the past tried to erase.

screenings.title: Making Marie Antoinette
screenings.description: In 2005, Eleanor Coppola filmed her daughter Sofia directing Marie Antoinette at the Palace of Versailles, the first production ever granted access to the palace. For two decades, eighty hours of footage went unseen. Now, twenty years after the film’s release and in fulfillment of her mother’s wish, that footage becomes a film of its own. Making Marie Antoinette follows the making of this landmark production, Milena Canonero’s costume work, and what it took to direct at 34, watched the whole time by her own mother.

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: The Social Reckoning
screenings.description: A companion piece to the hit film The Social Network, Sorkin’s original screenplay tells the true story of how Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a young Facebook engineer, enlists the help of Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a Wall Street Journal reporter, to go on a dangerous journey that ends up blowing the whistle on the social network’s most guarded secrets.

screenings.title: Virgina
screenings.description: When a fourth daughter is born to a family “cursed” by superstition to bear no male heirs, the decision is made to raise the child with a boy’s name—Stevan—as well as a man’s rights and responsibilities… though as Stevan passes adolescence, first love and a brush with personal tragedy will spark rebellion in his breast. An acutely observed study of a 19th-century peasant culture steeped in misogyny, and a strikingly sensual story of self-discovery, presented in a new 2K restoration in its NYC premiere.

screenings.title: All That Heaven Allows
screenings.description: Perhaps the very finest of Sirk’s Ross Hunter-produced melodramas, All That Heaven Allows pairs Jane Wyman and Rock Hudson as, respectively, a well-off widow in country club Connecticut, and the broad-necked, Thoreau-reading gardener who she falls for. Her priggish children, aghast, conspire to break off the pairing, an endeavor that ends in a bone-chilling Christmas conciliation—the presentation of a gift television set as a kind of death sentence. Of this scene Rainer Werner Fassbinder, profoundly marked by his encounter with Sirk’s film, would write: “At that point everyone in the moviehouse breaks down. They suddenly understand something about the world and what it does to people.” Right on.

Persona: 60th Anniversary Screening (Co-presented with NewFest)
screenings.description: Dir. Ingmar Bergman. 1966. 82 mins. Sweden. DCP. “If looked at through the right queer lens, Bergman’s Persona could be among the most penetrating break-up movies ever made.” With his landmark drama Persona, which celebrates its 60th anniversary this year, Ingmar Bergman reached new heights of visual poetry. Liv Ullmann, in her first of many legendary collaborations with Bergman, plays a stage actor who has inexplicably gone silent. Bibi Andersson is equally mesmerizing as the garrulous young nurse caring for her at a remote island cottage. Isolated together, the women perform a mysterious spiritual and emotional transference in a scene that has come to influence generations of filmmaking. Shot by the great Sven Nykvist, Persona remains a penetrating, dreamlike work of profound psychological depth that has long been discussed as a breakthrough tale of unspoken love. The Museum is pleased to co-present this masterpiece on the big screen with NewFest, New York’s Largest Queer Film Fest. Purchase tickets through NewFest’s website. Co-presented with:

screenings.title: Wildwood in 35mm
screenings.description: Wildwood is a handcrafted epic fantasy that transports audiences into a secret, dangerously alive world. A girl’s desperate quest to save her baby brother unfolds into a spectacular, high-stakes adventure through a forbidden forest full of enchanted creatures, endearing allies, and formidable adversaries—where an entire hidden realm hangs in the balance. In an era of automation, LAIKA delivers its most ambitious and globally accessible film yet—a bold fusion of human-crafted artistry and cinematic storytelling from the makers of Coraline.

screenings.title: Music Video Mischief with director Nigel Dick
screenings.description: 6:30–8:00 p.m. The art and style of rock music videos from the mid 1980s through the early 2000s—the choreography, the fashion, the swooning looks!—defined an era for millennials and GenX. Join us in the Bartos Screening Room to see a selection of ebullient music videos from director Nigel Dick. They include Britney Spears’s iconic “Baby One More Time” and Oasis’s “Wonderwall,” plus videos featuring Cher, Celine Dion, Tears for Fears, Guns N’ Roses, Alice Cooper, Def Leppard, and plenty of surprises, too! These videos show some of the chaos and charm of the era. This free screening will be followed by a conversation with Nigel Dick and Rolling Stone senior writer David Browne about the making of these classics and a book signing of Dick’s Music Video Mischief: Ozzy to Britney, Oasis to Gn’R, McCartney to Cher: a lifetime of rock and chaos (2026, Trouser Press Books), available for sale in the MoMI Shop (store closes at 8:00 p.m.). Free with RSVP. Special Guests: After a brief stint busking in the Paris Metro, Nigel Dick got his start in the music business at London’s upstart Stiff label in the late ’70s. He began a career as a music video director; ultimately working with hundreds of stars, including Oasis, Ozzy Osbourne, Cher, Paul McCartney, Guns n’ Roses, Toto, Britney Spears, Celine Dion, Alice Cooper, Def Leppard, Alice in Chains, and Tears for Fears. If you’ve ever watched MTV, you’ve seen his work. He has directed more than 450 music videos and 35+ documentaries and feature films. He has won three MTV awards, two Billboard Awards, three MVPA awards and one Brit award. His videos have been nominated for a further 21 MTV awards, 26 Much Music Awards, and a Grammy. His book Music Video Mischief is out on Trouser Press Books September 15. David Browne is a Senior Writer at Rolling Stone, where he contributes deep-dive reports, reviews and profiles on music. He is also the author of seven books, including biographies of Sonic Youth, Jeff Buckley, the Grateful Dead, and, most recently Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young: The Wild, Definitive Saga of Rock’s Greatest Supergroup.

screenings.description: See the uncut and unfiltered theatrical experience Ken Russell envisioned for his 1971 classic.

screenings.title: Fjord
screenings.description: From two-time Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, a Norwegian woman and her devout Romanian husband relocate with their five children to a remote, close-knit, coastal town. Their teenage children form a fast bond with a neighboring family as unease begins to simmer around their rigid beliefs. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgment that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

screenings.title: The Devils
screenings.description: Assembled from the original camera negative, this new 4K restoration presents Ken Russell’s definitive vision of The Devils by referencing the edit he privately constructed in 2004. The film’s sound has been remastered from original English Composite 35mm Mag Film, transferred at 96kHz, plus other original film elements in selected spots as needed. The Picture and Sound restoration was performed by Warner Bros. Post Production Creative Services, Water Tower Color, and Warner Bros. Sound.

screenings.description: Inspired by true events and the whistleblower who started the social media reckoning we’re seeing play out today, this Aaron Sorkin original screenplay is a companion piece to the hit film THE SOCIAL NETWORK and a true David and Goliath story. Frances Haugen (Madison), a young Facebook engineer, enlists the help of Jeff Horwitz (White), a Wall Street Journal reporter, to go on a dangerous journey that ends up blowing the whistle on the social network’s most guarded secrets.

screenings.title: Nosferatu + Live Score
screenings.description: Nosferatu + Live Score by the Andrew Alden Ensemble The vampire film that started them all gets its shadow back. The Andrew Alden Ensemble performs an original score live beneath F.W. Murnau’s 1922 landmark — the New York chamber group whose violin, cello, keys, drums, and voice sit somewhere between contemporary classical and rock, writing music built for the room rather than the recording booth: immediate, physical, and made for this film alone. On screen, Count Orlok (Max Schreck) uncoils out of the Carpathians — all talons and teeth and rat-borne plague — and crosses the sea toward a town that cannot wake from him. A hundred years later the images still crawl.

screenings.description: U.S., 1971 Directed by William Greaves Starring Patricia Ree Gilbert, Don Fellows, William Greaves, Bob Rosen Approx. 75 min. Screen tests are being shot in Central Park for the leads in a possible feature, while another crew films the filming of the tests, and a third films the first two in the context of life in the park going on around them. Avant-garde verité that slipped off the radar for 30 years. *With The First World Festival of Negro Arts U.S., 1966 Directed by William Greaves Approx. 40 min. 4K restoration. The official documentary film of the festival held in Dakar, Senegal in 1966, in which over 2,000 writers, artists, and performers from Africa and the African Diaspora participated. Featuring Duke Ellington, Langston Hughes, Alvin Ailey, Aimé Césaire, Leopold Senghor, and many other artists, performers, and dignitaries from thirty countries. “You have to realize that the reason why I went into motion pictures was to make films like The First World Festival of Negro Arts. It was the first opportunity I had to make films that expressed a black perspective on reality. Until then I had not had access to financing which would permit that.” – William Greaves 4K restoration by IndieCollect

screenings.description: Filmed over ten years, ONE IN A MILLION follows Israa from childhood to adulthood on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing bonds and reshaping her sense of self. Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, ONE IN A MILLION illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire

screenings.title: Bram Stoker’s Dracula
screenings.description: Dir. Francis Ford Coppola. 1992, 128 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Gary Oldman, Winona Ryder, Anthony Hopkins, Sadie Frost, Keanu Reeves, Tom Waits. In adapting the original Victorian-era Gothic vampire novel, Coppola pulled out all the stops and then some. For his rendition of the Dracula story, Coppola produced a quirky, idiosyncratic, and over-the-top cascade of lush and violent horror imagery that was, miraculously, a box-office smash. Working with brilliantly self-imposed limitations (all practical effects that would have been possible in the silent era); cramming every frame with monumental sets and matte paintings; and directing Oldman in one of his finest performances as the devilishly romantic Transylvanian count, Coppola created a film so sensational that even the notoriously horror-averse Academy Awards honored it three times, for makeup, sound effects, and Eiko Ishioka’s dazzling costumes. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Almost Famous
screenings.description: Before breaking into movies with his screenplay for Fast Times at Ridgemont High, Cameron Crowe was a teenage journalist with a regular byline in Rolling Stone magazine in the hedonistic early 1970s, and he draws from a deep well of memories of those pot-hazy days in his poignant-funny, semi-autobiographical Almost Famous, starring Patrick Fugit as a fresh-faced rock rag writer on the road with hesher idols Stillwater, Kate Hudson as road-warrior Stillwater superfan “Penny Lane,” and Philip Seymour Hoffman as an impassioned, opinionated, marvelously disheveled Lester Bangs.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

Carlos (Milo Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And Alberto (Carlos González) uncovers a long-buried family secret — one that finally gives voice to truths the past tried to erase.

screenings.description: U.S., 2005 Directed by William Greaves Starring William Greaves, Steve Buscemi, Audrey Heningham, Ndeye Ade Sokhna Approx. 99 min. “TAKE 2½ returns to the scene of the original experiment, creates a new scenario built upon the events of the past, and sets about another aggressive peeling away of artifice and falsity, not just in the performances but in the filmmaking itself. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgment that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

screenings.title: The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
screenings.description: Harry is an old-school hustler. A classic native New Yorker, he moves through life lubricating palms with cash, relying on his wits and connections. But times are changing for Harry. His daily pickpocket take isn’t green bills and wristwatches, it’s credit cards and cell phones. And one unfortunate night, cryptocurrency and a handgun. THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

A work of remarkable specificity and imagination, this inimitable, hot and bothered horror landmark is presented in a new 4K restoration.

screenings.title: Vampyr + Live Score
screenings.description: Carl Theodor Dreyer’s 1932 fever dream is less a horror film than a nightmare filmed at the moment of waking — fog, drifting shadows, a scythe, a burial seen from inside the coffin. The Andrew Alden Ensemble scores it live with violin, electric guitar, piano, synthesizers, and percussion, the New York group’s music moving with the film’s logic of dread rather than against it. A young traveler, Allan Gray (Julian West), arrives in a riverside village held under the spell of a vampire, and the world begins to come loose at the edges. Dreyer made it as sound cinema was being born and produced something stranger than either silence or speech; performed with a live original score, it turns stranger still.

In an era of automation, LAIKA delivers its most ambitious and globally accessible film yet—a bold fusion of human-crafted artistry and cinematic storytelling from the makers of Coraline.

Met with middling reviews during its original release, Prince of Darkness is now considered one of Carpenter’s greatest achievements in atmospheric terror and features another one of his classic synthesizer scores.

screenings.description: On the outskirts of a village by the sea, lives a Fisherwoman; smelly, single and perpetually ridiculed. One day, fed up with her stuffy, small-minded neighbors, she commissions herself a husband to be made from wicker. In an otherwise conservative town, this unconventional romance sparks outrage, jealousy and chaos.

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.description: Extracurricular-mad but otherwise unpromising 15-year-old student Max Fisher (Jason Schwartzman) is too busy competing (or so he thinks) with sad sack industrialist Bill Murray for the affections of teacher Olivia Williams to survive “sudden death academic probation” in Anderson’s deeply funny, deeply melancholic—and very class-conscious—sophomore feature. A back-to-school perennial, all dressed up in prep school navy blue and the muted colors of north Texas autumn, positively thrumming with the upstart energy of British Invasion anthems. (“Anderson,” noted admirer Martin Scorsese, “has a fine sense of how music works against an image.”) An irresistible, disarmingly original, delicately wrought comic fable.

screenings.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
screenings.description: An ardent aficionado of the work of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Cushing takes over the chambers at 221B Baker Street with aplomb and gives us a Sherlock for the ages in Fisher’s adaptation of the 1902 Holmes adventure of the same name, in which our hero is called to Dartmoor to investigate the mysterious death-by-fright of one Sir Charles Baskerville, leaving his estate in the hands of his heir and nephew, Henry (Christopher Lee). With the invaluable assistance of Jack Asher’s subdued Technicolor photography, Fisher wrings every drop of atmosphere out of Doyle’s tale of mist-shrouded moors and ancestral curses, making this one of Holmes’s very finest big-screen outings. (Special mention is due to Fisher’s ingenious use of child stand-ins for his leads to establish the terrible proportions of the eponymous mastiff.)

screenings.title: Corpse Bride
screenings.description: U.S./U.K., 2005 Directed by Tim Burton and Mike Johnson Starring Johnny Depp, Helena Bonham Carter Approx. 77 min. “‘By Jove, man, looks like we’ve got ourselves a breather!’ The cadaver’s patronising chortle says it all: being alive is nothing to shout about in this, the second stop-motion feature from Tim Burton. In an Orpheus-type story split between the maudlin, near-monochrome land of the living and a razzle-dazzle-’em underworld, it’s clear that the dead have more fun. In a nineteenth-century middle-European town, Victor (voiced by Johnny Depp), timid and sensitive son of grotesque nouveaux riches—he’s in fish—is lined up to marry Victoria (Emily Watson), heiress of some equally ghastly down-at-heel aristos. It’s a reasonable match—both look as if they’d faint at the slam of a door—but matters are complicated by Victor’s inadvertent betrothal to Emily (Helena Bonham Carter), a marriage-fixated corpse and not a bad sort, once you get used to the sight of her ribs twinkling through her decomposing bodice and the maggot that lives in her eye.” – Time Out

screenings.title: The Exorcist
screenings.description: When 12-year-old Regan MacNeil falls ill, she becomes violent and puzzles doctors with the personality of a horrifying entity. Desperate for answers, Regan’s movie-star mother Chris seeks the help of two priests: one who has lost his faith, and an exorcist. Winner of 1973 Oscars for Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Sound Mixing, THE EXORCIST remains one of the most shocking and gripping movies in the history of cinema.

screenings.title: Redline
screenings.description: In the distant future, hot-blooded, old-fashioned racer JP competes in Redline, a race to determine the fastest car in the galaxy. Alongside gifted mechanic Frisbie and fellow racer Sonoshee, he navigates friendship, love and high-speed competition in Takeshi Koike’s hand-drawn science-fiction adventure, seven years in the making.

screenings.title: Ju-On: The Grudge
screenings.description: A social worker visits an elderly woman at her house. The woman appears deeply disturbed, but that’s nothing compared to the shapeless black void — also known as “Kayako” — that lurks in an upstairs hallway. Quiet, creepy, and with bursts of unexpected intensity, JU-ON: THE GRUDGE combines liminal spaces and creepypasta chills to rattle your skeleton. There’s nothing scarier than not knowing what’s scaring you.

screenings.title: Grey Gardens
screenings.description: Meet Big and Little Edie Beale: mother and daughter, high-society dropouts, and reclusive cousins of Jackie Onassis. The two manage to thrive together amid the decay and disorder of their East Hampton, New York, mansion, making for an eerily ramshackle echo of the American Camelot. An impossibly intimate portrait, this 1976 documentary by Albert and David Maysles, codirected by Ellen Hovde and Muffie Meyer, quickly became a cult classic and established Little Edie as a fashion icon and philosopher queen.

screenings.title: Medea (1988)
screenings.description: Based on an unfilmed screenplay by Carl Theodor Dreyer and, of course, Euripides’s tragedy of the same title, von Trier’s made-for-television film—save for two epiphanic eruptions—is uncharacteristically austere, the enfant terrible of Danish cinema making himself a medium for the Old Master’s vision, setting the source material in a pre-Christian Denmark. “An experimental film in the true sense of the word… Taking the greatest limitation of video—the medium’s lack of depth of field—Mr. von Trier turns it into a strength, flattening perspectives in a way that collapses his foreground characters into the tumultuous backgrounds (waves, wind-swept fields) that surround and dominate them.” —Dave Kehr, The New York Times

screenings.title: La Bola Negra in 35mm

Carlos (Milo Quifes) longs to belong in a fractured Spain. Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) finds connection across enemy lines. And Alberto (Carlos González) uncovers a long-buried family secret — one that finally gives voice to truths the past tried to erase.

A girl’s desperate quest to save her baby brother unfolds into a spectacular, high-stakes adventure through a forbidden forest full of enchanted creatures, endearing allies, and formidable adversaries—where an entire hidden realm hangs in the balance. In an era of automation, LAIKA delivers its most ambitious and globally accessible film yet—a bold fusion of human-crafted artistry and cinematic storytelling from the makers of Coraline.

screenings.title: Winter of the Crow

Manville plays a British professor visiting Poland in 1981, who is suddenly swept up in extraordinary and dangerous events at the onset of the country’s Martial Law era. The film is a thrilling and immersive cat-and-mouse game, inspired by the short story by Booker Prize and Nobel Prize winning author Olga Tokarczuk.

Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: My Undesirable Friends: Part Ii – Exile: Chapters 1-3
screenings.description: CRITIC’S PICK. “Gripping... Expect to find yourself riveted... Grand in scale but entirely intimate in scope, what she’s achieved here is a landmark work that will go down as one of the boldest documentary achievements of the 21st century.” – Ryan Lattanzio, IndieWire “A riveting and vital portrait of media courage under fire. It’s as must-see as they get.” – Nick Schager, Daily Beast CRITIC’S PICK. “Essential. Riveting.” – Alissa Wilkinson, The New York Times “Monumental... It’s great cinema.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine/Vulture “The follow-up to 2024’s LAST AIR IN MOSCOW proves every bit as compelling, if more intimate... EXILE deepens the viewer’s connection to Loktev’s journalists while introducing engaging new subjects... Funny, resilient, and vibrant, Loktev’s subjects have lost their home but not their defiant spirit.” – Tim Grierson, Screen “RIVETING. A globetrotting journey that proves harrowing in unexpected ways over an engrossing five chapters... Loktev and co-editor Michael Taylor have crafted a conversational epic that imbues each twist and turn with enormous stakes... Speaking truth to power with the online tools at their disposal, this murderer’s row consists of lively, awkward, driven, beautiful, lovestruck, and above-all complicated people, all caught in impossible personal and professional deadlocks and weighed down by immigrant uncertainty.” – Siddhant Adlakha, Variety “STAGGERING. GRIPPING. [A] massive monument to journalism, competing in length and ambition with legendary feats of nonfiction like SHOAH and the UP series... a celebration of truth in an endless fight against deception.” – Jacob Oller, AV Club “An essential chronicle of reporters under fire... Loktev, who shot the entire 12-hour doc herself, turns each reporter into the character of a real-life series unfolding before our eyes as the years go by and the war inevitably drags on... [she] creates an intimacy that goes beyond the international crises and political upheavals to focus on the human costs of an unending conflict.” – Jordan Mintzer, The Hollywood Reporter “CHILLING. The film’s final chapter has the charge of an espionage thriller.” – Marshall Shaffer, Slant “BRILLIANT. Keeping us on the edge of our seats for 6 hours. screenings.title: Vampire’s Kiss
screenings.description: Dir. Robert Bierman. 1988, 103 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Nicolas Cage, Maria Conchita Alonso, Jennifer Beals, Kasi Lemmons, Elizabeth Ashley. This eighties comedy-horror freakout gave Nicolas Cage one of his most whacked-out roles, as a New York City yuppie literary agent who descends into cockroach-eating madness after believing he’s fallen for a sexy vampire (Jennifer Beals). Coming right of Moonstruck (which this movie also could have been titled!), Cage gives a genuinely weird, entirely committed, and gratifyingly berserk performance—the kind of high-wire acting that is a true special effect all its own. Set among the high-rises of midtown Manhattan and the downtown nightclub scene,Vampire’s Kiss is quintessential ’80s New York mayhem. screenings.description: From two-time Palme d’Or winner Cristian Mungiu, a Norwegian woman and her devout Romanian husband relocate with their five children to a remote, close-knit, coastal town. Their teenage children form a fast bond with a neighboring family as unease begins to simmer around their rigid beliefs. When allegations of abuse emerge, they are forced to confront a system of judgment that blurs the line between concern and prejudice.

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.description: Ozu’s satirical—and ultimately quite touching—portrait of a marriage first seen in a state of quiet unraveling stars Kogure Michiyo and Saburi Shin as a well-off, childless middle-aged couple who find discreet outlets to express their disappointments and resentments towards one another: the Westernized wife through habitual practice of harmless deceptions and put-downs of the husband that she likens to a sluggish carp in a koi pond; her husband by supporting a niece (Keiko Tsushima) in her flight from proposed marriage arrangement interviews.

screenings.title: Elisa, My Life

An intoxicating whorl of memory, fantasy—in his literary output Luis dwells on his daughter’s imagined life, depicted here along with her own daydreams—and hard-to-swallow reality, in which an act of mandatory “reconciliation” becomes an unveiling of terrible, naked grief. “As in all of her Saura films, [Chaplin] reveals qualities of feeling, control and beauty that no other directors have ever found.” —The New York Times

screenings.title: One in a Million
screenings.description: Filmed over ten years, ONE IN A MILLION follows Israa from childhood to adulthood on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing bonds and reshaping her sense of self. Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, ONE IN A MILLION illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

screenings.title: First We Bombed New Mexico - the Aftermath
screenings.description: The inspiring story of a relentless Latina cancer survivor who takes on 80 years of injustice by the U.S. government. Tina Cordova catalyzes a movement to secure acknowledgement and compensation for the ignored Native American and Hispanic cancer victims of the Trinity Bomb’s radioactive fallout. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH exposes the racism and nuclear colonization that enabled New Mexico to become America’s nuclear bomb–making state. The film screens during a moment of grave global insecurity. This film personalizes the unthinkable human cost of another nuclear incident. An earlier version of the film won 16 festival awards, including Best Director and Best Documentary at the Paris Cine Film Festival, Best Documentary Feature and Best Directing at the Worldwide Women’s Film Festival, and the Jury Prize for Best Historical Documentary at the San Antonio Film Festival. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH reveals an unknown story that has captured audiences. The film was a part of the momentum that led to Congress awarding compensation to New Mexico Downwinder families in 2025. The inspirational re-release witnesses a people who were once considered powerless and voiceless finally gaining recognition after years of fighting for justice.

But an airplane incident lands him in the middle of a grotesque amusement park, where he is transformed into a member of its expansive freak show. A deliriously grotesque live-action cartoon, Freaked is a carnivalesque melange of eye-popping make-up effects and fun-house set design. It also features an all-star cameo casting ranging from Gibby Haynes of The Butthole Surfers to Mr. T, plus masked appearances from Keanu Reeves and future Wicked director Jon M. Chu. Must be seen to be believed.

Greaves’s idea was to use a Moreno-trained psychodramatist, Walter Klavun, to create a sociodrama to deal with racial conflict within the workplace. His approach proved to be novel for a sponsored film.” – J. J. Murphy, William Greaves, Filmmaking as Mission (Columbia University Press, 2021) 4K digital transfer by IndieCollect. Presented with support from The Richard Brick, Geri Ashur, and Sara Bershtel Fund for Social Justice Documentaries Wealth of a Nation U.S., 1966 Directed by William Greaves Approx. 21 min. 4K restoration. Commissioned by the United States Information Agency to produce a documentary on freedom of speech, director William Greaves profiled several artists—including avant-garde sculptor Lee Bontecou, free-jazz trumpeter Bill Dixon, and futurist architect William Katavolos—to explore how audacious self-expression can move a society toward higher ideals. Even in this short industrial-film format, Greaves draws on virtuoso camera work and lyrical montage to communicate a signature theme: the deeply reciprocal relationship between creative individuals and their communities. 4K restoration by IndieCollect. Presented with support from The Richard Brick, Geri Ashur, and Sara Bershtel Fund for Social Justice Documentaries and The Roy Lichtenstein Foundation Fund

screenings.title: The Exorcist
screenings.description: Dir. William Friedkin. 1973, 122 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Ellen Burstyn, Linda Blair, Jason Miller, Max von Sydow. Widely considered one of the scariest films ever made, The Exorcist has shocked and fascinated generations of viewers. Directed by William Friedkin and written by William Peter Blatty, adapting his own best-selling 1971 novel, the film made an essential contribution to the horror genre, pitting the Catholic church against a demon for control of a young girl’s soul. The film’s remarkable, often shocking effects were done by the brilliant and pioneering makeup master Dick Smith (Little Big Man, The Godfather), who transformed the possessed young girl Regan (Linda Blair) into a foul, blasphemous monster. Nominated for ten Academy Awards, including Best Picture, and winning for Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Sound. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. screenings.title: Peppermint Frappé
screenings.description: Chaplin and Saura’s electric creative partnership began with this perverse play on Alfred Hitchcock’s (already quite perverse!) Vertigo, in which meek doctor José Luis López Vázquez becomes besotted with his childhood friend’s bride (Chaplin), and sets about making over a doting assistant (Chaplin, again) at the radiology clinic where he works into the image of the woman he yearns for but cannot have. A delirious and seriously deviant psychological thriller. “I got home quite late and turned on the television; a film in Spanish with subtitles, that I knew absolutely nothing about... It was hard for me to follow and understand but, at the same time, I was convinced it was the film of a great director. I watched the rest of the film glued to the TV set and when it was over I picked up a newspaper and saw that it was Peppermint Frappé.” —Stanley Kubrick

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? Many of the revelations in the film were published almost immediately as we learned of them, in the months following the October 7th attacks, by The Guardian (one of NAZA’s producers), in collaboration with reporting partners +972 Magazine and Local Call. The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: Something Special (Willy/Milly)
screenings.description: Frustrated by a world in which boys seem to get the best of everything, 14-year-old Milly (Pamela Adlon) makes a wish to swap her sex, and wakes up to find her—or, rather, his—wish has come true. “In my obsession with Something Special, I purchased this 35mm print of it almost 30 years ago. There are a handful of ‘teenage girls passing as boys’ films (She’s the Man is probably the best known). In so many films with gender-crossing characters, the passing is so unconvincing that it renders the film ultimately unsatisfying for a queer audience. But Pamela Adlon’s performance here as Willy is absolutely spectacular.” —Series curator Jenni Olson, queer film historian and archivist

screenings.title: Making Marie Antoinette
screenings.description: In 2005, Eleanor Coppola filmed her daughter Sofia directing Marie Antoinette at the Palace of Versailles, the first production ever granted access to the palace. For two decades, eighty hours of footage went unseen. Now, twenty years after the film’s release and in fulfillment of her mother’s wish, that footage becomes a film of its own. Making Marie Antoinette follows the making of this landmark production, Milena Canonero’s costume work, and what it took to direct at 34, watched the whole time by her own mother.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: First We Bombed New Mexico - the Aftermath
screenings.description: The inspiring story of a relentless Latina cancer survivor who takes on 80 years of injustice by the U.S. government. Tina Cordova catalyzes a movement to secure acknowledgement and compensation for the ignored Native American and Hispanic cancer victims of the Trinity Bomb’s radioactive fallout. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH exposes the racism and nuclear colonization that enabled New Mexico to become America’s nuclear bomb–making state. The film screens during a moment of grave global insecurity. This film personalizes the unthinkable human cost of another nuclear incident. An earlier version of the film won 16 festival awards, including Best Director and Best Documentary at the Paris Cine Film Festival, Best Documentary Feature and Best Directing at the Worldwide Women’s Film Festival, and the Jury Prize for Best Historical Documentary at the San Antonio Film Festival. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH reveals an unknown story that has captured audiences. The film was a part of the momentum that led to Congress awarding compensation to New Mexico Downwinder families in 2025. The inspirational re-release witnesses a people who were once considered powerless and voiceless finally gaining recognition after years of fighting for justice.

screenings.title: Miss Representation: Rise Up
screenings.description: Over a decade after MISS REPRESENTATION exposed the media’s contribution to the underrepresentation of women in leadership, this follow-up dives deep into the cultural backlash against women’s agency and power. With the proliferation of AI and deepfakes, a new era of tech-facilitated violence is exacerbating sexism and misogyny in an attempt to control and silence women and girls. With inspiring young women at its core, MISS REPRESENTATION: RISE UP interweaves their personal journeys with powerful voices in media, culture, leadership, and academia to reimagine a future that finally uplifts women and girls.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire

THE ONLY LIVING PICKPOCKET IN NEW YORK is a nostalgic portrait of a small-time career criminal navigating today's digitally networked world. Writer/Director Noah Segan's modern metropolis is powered by the ephemera of a time gone by, with shoe-leather action brought to radiant life by a terrific cast, led by John Turturro's exceptional turn as Harry.

One day, fed up with her stuffy, small-minded neighbors, she commissions herself a husband to be made from wicker. In an otherwise conservative town, this unconventional romance sparks outrage, jealousy and chaos.

screenings.description: Screaming Mad George’s sole directorial feature is a tokusatsu film about a guy who finds an alien suit that turns him into a superpowered cyber-bug. This puts him on a collision course against a shadowy mega-corp called Chronos and a slimy, reptilian race known as the Zoanoids, who get mad and kidnap his girlfriend. With the help of rogue CIA agent Mark Hamill, it’s up to The Guyver to rescue the girl, take down the man, and save the planet. Co-directed with adrenaline junkie Steve Wang (1997’s Drive), The Guyver is a fantastic showcase for SMG’s icky creature effects.

screenings.title: Demonic Umbrella Aka Midnight Conjure
screenings.description: The two films, THE CHINESE GHOSTBUSTER and EXORCIST MASTER (the latter screened as part of our 2023 Fist Fright Marathon) would mark the last time Lam would appear on the big screen as his Taoist priest character, and curiously, both films provide a more in-depth look at Taoist ritual and practice than most of his previous appearances. CHINESE GHOSTBUSTER is largely a riff on the Taoist folk legend of Zhong Kui, a mythological demon slayer known as the “King of Ghosts”, while EXORCIST MASTER operates on a playful contrast between the religious traditions of its two leads, a Taoist priest played by Lam, and a Christian priest played by Wu. Together the films offer a fittingly spiritual coda to the career of a performer whose likeness inadvertently became synonymous with the Taoism itself.

screenings.description: Dir. John Landis. 1981, 97 mins. U.S. DCP. With David Naughton, Griffin Dunne, Jenny Agutter. The rare humor-tinged horror that manages to be entirely terrifying and quite funny, Landis’s film follows two American backpackers whose destinies are changed forever when they decide to stray from the roads while traveling across rural England. After being bitten by a strange furry animal, David Kessler (Naughton) wakes up in a London hospital and finds himself plagued by ominous dreams and foreboding ghosts telling him to beware the next full moon. Rick Baker’s eye-popping practical makeup effects (which won an Oscar the first year the Academy added a makeup category) enhance this marvelous dark comedy that still has the power to make audiences scream and giggle. Griffin Dunne appears in an unforgettable supporting role as David’s friend, whose death can’t stop him from trying to hang out. screenings.title: Fugs Film!
screenings.description: Formed in late 1964 by Ed Sanders and Tuli Kupferberg, alongside drummer Ken Weaver – anarchic East Village beat poets who could barely play their instruments – The Fugs are credited as the first true underground band. Their lo-fi folk music could be challenging and weird but they had a knack for catchy pop songs, such as “Supergirl” and ‘Slum Goddess”. One of the most crucial figures in countercultural history, Sanders founded the Peace Eye bookstore and the arts journal “F*** You: A Magazine of the Arts”, and, among other late-1960s antics, attempted to levitate the Pentagon and staged a funeral for flower power in San Francisco. Chuck Smith’s vital documentary features eye-popping archival footage and interviews with Sanders, Aline & R. Crumb, Lenny Kaye, Penny Arcade, Jeffrey Lewis, and many others, to tell the story of NYC’s original punks.The screening will be followed by a Q&A with Penny Arcade, Steven Taylor and other participants from the film!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: First We Bombed New Mexico - the Aftermath
screenings.description: The inspiring story of a relentless Latina cancer survivor who takes on 80 years of injustice by the U.S. government. Tina Cordova catalyzes a movement to secure acknowledgement and compensation for the ignored Native American and Hispanic cancer victims of the Trinity Bomb’s radioactive fallout. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH exposes the racism and nuclear colonization that enabled New Mexico to become America’s nuclear bomb–making state. The film screens during a moment of grave global insecurity. This film personalizes the unthinkable human cost of another nuclear incident. An earlier version of the film won 16 festival awards, including Best Director and Best Documentary at the Paris Cine Film Festival, Best Documentary Feature and Best Directing at the Worldwide Women’s Film Festival, and the Jury Prize for Best Historical Documentary at the San Antonio Film Festival. FIRST WE BOMBED NEW MEXICO - THE AFTERMATH reveals an unknown story that has captured audiences. The film was a part of the momentum that led to Congress awarding compensation to New Mexico Downwinder families in 2025. The inspirational re-release witnesses a people who were once considered powerless and voiceless finally gaining recognition after years of fighting for justice.

screenings.title: Naza
screenings.description: We made this film out of a sense of obligation to use our position as Israeli filmmakers and journalists to examine the systems behind the mass killing of Palestinian civilians for which our country is responsible. While filming members of Israel’s military on rooftops at night in Tel Aviv over the past three years, we found ourselves asking the very questions that were asked by our grandparents’ generation and throughout the 20th century: how does one group of people allow the total dehumanization of another? What do the inner workings of such a system look like? The film lets us explore something deeper than we could in our investigative journalism alone: not only the words being said but also those that are not said, the silence. It is up to all of us to break that silence.

screenings.title: One in a Million
screenings.description: Filmed over ten years, ONE IN A MILLION follows Israa from childhood to adulthood on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing bonds and reshaping her sense of self. Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, ONE IN A MILLION illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

screenings.title: Making Marie Antoinette
screenings.description: In 2005, Eleanor Coppola filmed her daughter Sofia directing Marie Antoinette at the Palace of Versailles, the first production ever granted access to the palace. For two decades, eighty hours of footage went unseen. Now, twenty years after the film’s release and in fulfillment of her mother’s wish, that footage becomes a film of its own. Making Marie Antoinette follows the making of this landmark production, Milena Canonero’s costume work, and what it took to direct at 34, watched the whole time by her own mother.

screenings.title: October Country
screenings.description: Shot over the course of a year (beginning and ending on Halloween), OCTOBER COUNTRY is a vérité-style documentary that follows members of the Mosher family, a working-class family in upstate New York as they reconcile with the hardships of their daily life that includes unplanned pregnancy, sibling estrangement, poverty, emotional despondency and war trauma. October Country examines and provides insight into the fraught intergenerational cycles that can pervade in blue collar households.

screenings.title: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother
screenings.description: From writer-director Bassam Tariq, YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER YOUR MOTHER stars Mahershala Ali as Latif, a devoutly religious hitman who struggles to balance work, faith and fatherhood. When his wife dies, he embarks on a desperate journey across Houston to protect his children, confronting the forces closing in around him - and the beliefs threatening to unravel within.

screenings.title: The Social Reckoning
screenings.description: A companion piece to the hit film The Social Network, Sorkin’s original screenplay tells the true story of how Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a young Facebook engineer, enlists the help of Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), a Wall Street Journal reporter, to go on a dangerous journey that ends up blowing the whistle on the social network’s most guarded secrets.

screenings.title: Mikey and Nicky
screenings.description: “A dark dazzler… Over the course of one evening, the two pass an entire lifetime together talking, walking and waiting for the inevitable. Like all May’s films, has the hard-to-capture feeling of spontaneous life.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “May was known for her comedy but here proves absolutely fluent in the language of mobster lowlife, with an edge of caustic, disillusioned humor, and strange yet shockingly real outbursts of violence... This is a stag-rutting choreography of the emotions, with a sour smell of lonely defeated men, a tang of being up all night with cigarettes and beer.” – Peter Bradshaw, The Guardian “May might be the least sentimental woman storyteller since Flannery O’Connor in her stark refusal to sweeten the pill. If her relentless realism evokes the epic sweep of Erich von Stroheim’s GREED, her narrative still manages to cram a lifetime of troubled friendship, rivalry, money, and pain into the vicissitudes of a single night.” – Jonathan Rosenbaum

screenings.description: From acclaimed director Francis Ford Coppola, MEGALOPOLIS is a Roman Epic fable is set in an imagined Modern America. The City of New Rome must change, causing conflict between Cesar Catilina, a genius artist who seeks to leap into a utopian, idealistic future, and his opposition, Mayor Franklyn Cicero, who remains committed to a regressive status quo, perpetuating greed, special interests, and partisan warfare. Torn between them is socialite Julia Cicero, the mayor’s daughter, whose love for Cesar has divided her loyalties, forcing her to discover what she truly believes humanity deserves.

screenings.title: Tron
screenings.description: The cross-breeding of video games and cinema began in earnest with Tron, one of the first films to extensively employ CGI, here depicting the darkly glittering digital world inside a mainframe computer that programmer Jeff Bridges must compete in a series of gladiatorial contests in order to escape.

screenings.title: Once Upon a Time in Harlem
screenings.description: “One of the greatest cinematic works of creative nonfiction that I've ever seen.” – Richard Brody, The New Yorker CRITIC’S PICK. “A house party for the ages... A blissout and one of the events of this cinematic season... A deeply personal, collectively produced oral history of a specific moment of time as it was lived—and held in memory—by specific individuals. The past comes vibrantly alive in these rooms, but always circles back to the present and often points to the future... One of the sustaining pleasures of this wonderful, spirit-lifting movie is that—even with many of its contributors now gone—it feels excitingly alive.” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “A MASTERPIECE... A truly monumental work of art.” – Bilge Ebiri, New York Magazine “The stuff of legend... Feels like a miracle.” – Robert Daniels, RogerEbert.com “An atmospheric, electrifying documentary, and a moving testament to the importance of remembering.” – Shirley Li, The Atlantic “An intergenerational feat... A documentary brimming with the wise, the thought-provoking and the deeply entertaining... [A] glimmering gift... with something that resembles a calling forth of the ancestors... A vivid and layered time capsule... Turns viewers into time travelers but also invited guests, rightly grateful to be in the room. For some of us, this film might evoke the wonder of a great-grandchild listening in on grown-up reminiscences. Nodding at the substance. Smiling at the style.” – Lisa Kennedy, Variety “[A] rich doc crafted from gorgeously restored footage. A triumph of DIY filmmaking and an act of cinematic resistance.” – Jourdain Searles, The Hollywood Reporter “A masterpiece.” – David Fear, Rolling Stone “Not only the biggest surprise of this year’s Sundance, but a revelation.” – Chris O’Falt, IndieWire
screenings.director: David Greaves Conceived And Filmed By William Greaves

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

Awaiting the guillotine, Victor Frankenstein (Peter Cushing) ruminates on the catastrophic fallout of his attempt at creating an exemplary being from scavenged bits of the dead, which results in his cracked creation (Christopher Lee) going on a murderous rampage. Extravagantly colorful, generous with the gruesomeness, and performed with zest—all the hallmarks of Hammer in its prime are in place here, in a shining new 4K restoration.

screenings.description: The two films, THE CHINESE GHOSTBUSTER and EXORCIST MASTER (the latter screened as part of our 2023 Fist Fright Marathon) would mark the last time Lam would appear on the big screen as his Taoist priest character, and curiously, both films provide a more in-depth look at Taoist ritual and practice than most of his previous appearances. CHINESE GHOSTBUSTER is largely a riff on the Taoist folk legend of Zhong Kui, a mythological demon slayer known as the “King of Ghosts”, while EXORCIST MASTER operates on a playful contrast between the religious traditions of its two leads, a Taoist priest played by Lam, and a Christian priest played by Wu. screenings.description: While so many special effects spectacles are lost in time like tears in the rain, Blade Runner remains the template for imagining the neon-wreathed downer of the future, every bit as influential in its vision as was Fritz Lang’s Metropolis over a half century before. Working from a novel by cult writer Philip K. Dick to create a film that would become the gold standard for sci-fi noir, director Scott shares credit here with “visual futurist” Syd Mead’s design concepts and synth pioneer Vangelis’s atmospheric score.

screenings.description: In 2006, To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen sets out to make television history.

screenings.title: You Can See Everything
screenings.description: Thirty-four days before she's sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move.

screenings.title: Tetsuo: The Iron Man
screenings.description: That the world of the future was to be increasingly shaped by Asia was a central tenet of cyberpunk, and so it should come as no surprise that one of the greatest of cyberpunk films came from the Land of the Rising Sun. Man and machine feel the urge to merge in Tsukamoto’s utterly indescribable midnight movie staple, an assault-on-the-senses body horror running of the gauntlet which centers on an anonymous salaryman who begins to transform himself into a man of steel, his waking nightmare captured in twitchy camerawork and lurid, gritty black-and-white 16mm. A symphony of sex, steel, and scarification, set to a scraping industrial clangor.

screenings.title: The Exorcist
screenings.description: When 12-year-old Regan MacNeil falls ill, she becomes violent and puzzles doctors with the personality of a horrifying entity. Desperate for answers, Regan’s movie-star mother Chris seeks the help of two priests: one who has lost his faith, and an exorcist. Winner of 1973 Oscars for Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Sound Mixing, THE EXORCIST remains one of the most shocking and gripping movies in the history of cinema.

screenings.title: Redline
screenings.description: In the distant future, hot-blooded, old-fashioned racer JP competes in Redline, a race to determine the fastest car in the galaxy. Alongside gifted mechanic Frisbie and fellow racer Sonoshee, he navigates friendship, love and high-speed competition in Takeshi Koike’s hand-drawn science-fiction adventure, seven years in the making.

screenings.title: Ju-On: The Grudge
screenings.description: A social worker visits an elderly woman at her house. The woman appears deeply disturbed, but that’s nothing compared to the shapeless black void — also known as “Kayako” — that lurks in an upstairs hallway. Quiet, creepy, and with bursts of unexpected intensity, JU-ON: THE GRUDGE combines liminal spaces and creepypasta chills to rattle your skeleton. There’s nothing scarier than not knowing what’s scaring you.

screenings.title: Grey Gardens
screenings.description: Meet Big and Little Edie Beale: mother and daughter, high-society dropouts, and reclusive cousins of Jackie Onassis. The two manage to thrive together amid the decay and disorder of their East Hampton, New York, mansion, making for an eerily ramshackle echo of the American Camelot. An impossibly intimate portrait, this 1976 documentary by Albert and David Maysles, codirected by Ellen Hovde and Muffie Meyer, quickly became a cult classic and established Little Edie as a fashion icon and philosopher queen.

screenings.title: You Sorta Know It's Gonna End
screenings.description: From staples of the independent Canadian scene, filmmakers Kalil Haddad and Ryan Steel present the US premiere of their new shorts cycle You Sorta Know It’s Gonna End, a tangle of nostalgia, masculine crisis and caustic youth. THE GREAT EXPERIMENT is an epic poem in documentary form – a mirror held to an American nation at war with its own reflection, asking not who is right, but whether the experiment itself can survive.

screenings.title: Art Cinema for Tots: How to Play a Film
screenings.description: Born out of a commitment to the idea that it’s never too early to introduce kids to the pleasures of movies made outside of the commercial mainstream—and the suspicion that young audiences are often more open-minded and curious than their elders when it comes to such matters—Metrograph presents the latest iteration of Art Cinema for Tots, a celebration of handcrafted, kid-friendly films that reconcile the smart and the silly. Pennebaker’s document of a trip to the Central Park Zoo, and Francis Alÿs’s Reel/Unreel, which observes the game-playing of a group of Kabul children.

screenings.title: The Addams Family
screenings.description: Among the most perfectly cast Hollywood studio films of the last half-century, cinematographer-cum-director Sonnenfeld’s adaptation of Charles Addams’s macabre recurring New Yorker feature stars Raul Julia as the suave patriarch of the Addams clan (“You lady-killer…” “Acquitted!”), Anjelica Huston as his waxen, witchy bride, and an outstanding preadolescent Christina Ricci as doomy daughter Wednesday. A drolly dark comedy that moves with the fearsome speed of a 1930s screwball, thanks to the surgical precision of Dede Allen’s editing.

screenings.title: Young Frankenstein
screenings.description: A young neurosurgeon inherits the castle of his grandfather, the famous Dr. Victor von Frankenstein. In the castle he finds a funny hunchback called Igor, a pretty lab assistant named Inga and the old housekeeper, Frau Blucher. Young Frankenstein believes that the work of his grandfather was delusional, but when he discovers the book where the mad doctor described his reanimation experiment, he suddenly changes his mind.

screenings.title: Possible Love
