screenings.title: The Trouble with Harry
screenings.description: The inconvenient corpse, imbued with a sense of tragedy and terror in Hitchcock’s Rope, is the source of borderline-surrealist farce in The Trouble with Harry, his adaptation of Jack Trevor Story’s novel of the same name, a darkly comic tale in which the residents of a small New England hamlet—exteriors were shot on location in Vermont, with the fall foliage radiant in Technicolor—try and repeatedly fail to dispose of a dead body that has appeared in their midst. A rare foray into comedy (albeit of the black variety) for Hitchcock, with Shirley MacLaine, Mildred Natwick, and Jerry “The Beaver” Mathers perfectly embodying a bevy of smalltown American “types.”

screenings.title: News From Home
screenings.description: Akerman was 26 years old and living in New York City, away from her native Belgium and her mother, when she teamed with DP Babette Mangolte to film this diary/essay/poem in subway stations and on street corners, their images to eventually be paired with Akerman’s recitals of her mother’s fretful letters. Arguably this extraordinary filmmaker’s most perfect and poignant nonfiction work, both one of the greatest portraits of a city ever put on film and a troubling, touching depiction of maternal love. Screens in the English-language version.

screenings.title: Ec: Man of Aran
screenings.description: Flaherty’s third major film portrays the lives of a family of fisher folk on the Aran Islands off the coast of Galway, Ireland. Flaherty selected the location and subjects because of their isolation as the westernmost outpost of European civilization. In addition, the daily struggle between the islanders and the sea perfectly suited his interests and concerns. The scenes at sea are breathtaking.“His passionate devotion to the portrayal of human gesture and of a man’s fight for his family makes the film an incomparable account of human dignity. Better than anyone, Flaherty knew how to show the true face of Man.” –Georges Sadoul

screenings.title: Occupational Hazard: the First Coral Reefers
screenings.description: OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD: THE FIRST CORAL REEFERS is a feature documentary that journeys back to the 1970s and early 1980s to tell the story of Jimmy Buffett’s original Coral Reefer Band. Set against the creative backdrop of Key West, the film explores the musicians, friendships, touring years, and studio sessions that helped shape Buffett’s legendary sound. Through rare, never-before-seen archival footage and deeply personal interviews with founding members, tour managers, producers and music legends, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD captures the camaraderie, chaos, and magic of an era that thrived on freedom and lived without a rulebook. Narrated by Academy-award winner Jeff Bridges, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD offers fans a deeper look at the people behind the music and the era that helped define Jimmy Buffett’s lasting legacy. This film is a tribute to Buffett and the original Coral Reefers, the places and people that shaped them, the volatile beauty of a musical moment that couldn’t last but changed everything and their candid sentiment toward Buffett. It’s the origin story upon which the Parrot Head empire was built upon, by the people who helped lay the foundation.

screenings.title: Halloween
screenings.description: Credited, rightfully, as the film that kickstarted the “slasher” subgenre, Carpenter’s 1978 Halloween is a masterwork of building tension, an exercise in mood and suspense that takes its cues from Hitchcock, unlike most of the 80s gorefests it would inspire. The film’s key innovation – besides the indelibly terrifying image of the blank-faced “shape” aka Michael Myers – is setting it in an innocuous American suburb; there’s nowhere, not even a nice middle class home, where the viewer is safe. Jamie Lee Curtis makes her scream queen debut as one of several babysitters being stalked by a masked, escaped mental patient on Halloween night, her only savior being the patient’s maniacally driven doctor, played with gusto by the great Donald Pleasance. But the secret weapon of Halloween is the score – composed by Carpenter himself – a tinkling, off-meter piano figure that continues to haunt long after the final unsettling frame. A Halloween season perennial.

screenings.title: Prince of Darkness
screenings.description: The second film in John Carpenter’s unofficial apocalypse trilogy, Prince of Darkness stars Carpenter veteran Donald Pleasence as a priest who enlists a group of scientists and graduate students to investigate a mysterious cylinder in a Los Angeles church that might be connected to an ancient evil force. Met with middling reviews during its original release, Prince of Darkness is now considered one of Carpenter’s greatest achievements in atmospheric terror and features another one of his classic synthesizer scores.

Dick to create a film that would become the gold standard for sci-fi noir, director Scott shares credit here with “visual futurist” Syd Mead’s design concepts and synth pioneer Vangelis’s atmospheric score.

screenings.description: Dir. Adrien Beau. 2023, 90 mins. France, DCP. With Kacey Mottet Klein, Ariane Labed, Grégoire Colin, Vassili Schneider. A genuinely eccentric spin on the vampire story, integrating uncanny puppet effects with its live-action storytelling, this unsettling, lovingly crafted—and often funny—period creep-show adapts “The Family of the Vourdalak,” a novella by Aleksey Konstantinovich Tolstoy written in 1839—that’s nearly 60 years before Bram Stoker’s Dracula. Lost in a misty forest on a royal errand, the foppish Marquis d’Urfé, a diplomatic envoy for the King, happens upon a Serbian family’s home for shelter. Their village ransacked by the Turks, the clan nervously awaits the return of its patriarch, who has been gone six days to fight the enemy; upon his return, he has decidedly transformed into something both more and less than human. Adrien Beau’s ingenious twist on vampire folklore has the genuine feel of a classic horror short story, while its daring marionette effects and widescreen, super 16mm cinematography create a singularly eerie experience. screenings.description: Cherished by no less a personage than Martin Scorsese for its “totally uncalled for” graphic violence, The Curse of Frankenstein was a watershed film for both Fisher and Hammer, earning 30 times its budget back in the US alone and establishing the studio as the world’s preeminent purveyor of Gothic horror. Awaiting the guillotine, Victor Frankenstein (Peter Cushing) ruminates on the catastrophic fallout of his attempt at creating an exemplary being from scavenged bits of the dead, which results in his cracked creation (Christopher Lee) going on a murderous rampage. Extravagantly colorful, generous with the gruesomeness, and performed with zest—all the hallmarks of Hammer in its prime are in place here, in a shining new 4K restoration.

screenings.title: Beetlejuice
screenings.description: With her delivery of the line “My whole life is a dark room… One. Big. Dark. Room,” Winona Ryder cemented herself as a goth girl heroine for the ages, a brooding teen in widow’s weeds relocated by her parents to a creaky country house that happens to be haunted by the unquiet spirits of owners Alec Baldwin and Geena Davis, egged on in mischief-making by Michael Keaton’s Ghost with the Most, whose own hidden motives are rather more malevolent. “A bugaboo farce… Has a kid’s delight in the homegrown surreal… Michael Keaton has never been so uninhibited a comic.”—Pauline Kael, The New Yorker

screenings.title: Silent Night, Deadly Night 5: The Toy Maker | The Surreal Nightmares of Screaming Mad George
screenings.description: The series curator’s dark horse pick for must-see movie in the Screaming Mad George retrospective, the late entry from the direct-to-video years of the long, byzantine Christmas series is shockingly entertaining. The story involves a young boy who is traumatized when bizarre mystery toys kill people including his deadbeat father, his school bully, and a landlord (yes!) in strange and gruesome ways. This puts him in touch with a toy seller named Joe Petto—owner of “Petto’s Toys” (say it out loud)—played by a typically unhinged late-career Mickey Rooney. And from there, the story takes a twist into being a… Terminator knock-off? To the best of our knowledge, Silent Night, Deadly Night 5: The Toy Maker has never screened theatrically in New York City on 35mm.

screenings.title: The Exorcist
screenings.description: Dir. William Friedkin. 1973, 122 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Ellen Burstyn, Linda Blair, Jason Miller, Max von Sydow. Widely considered one of the scariest films ever made, The Exorcist has shocked and fascinated generations of viewers. Directed by William Friedkin and written by William Peter Blatty, adapting his own best-selling 1971 novel, the film made an essential contribution to the horror genre, pitting the Catholic church against a demon for control of a young girl’s soul. The film’s remarkable, often shocking effects were done by the brilliant and pioneering makeup master Dick Smith (Little Big Man, The Godfather), who transformed the possessed young girl Regan (Linda Blair) into a foul, blasphemous monster. Nominated for ten Academy Awards, including Best Picture, and winning for Best Adapted Screenplay and Best Sound. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. screenings.title: Vera
screenings.description: “When Caden Mark Gardner and I co-curated Vera as part of the original Masc series in 2022, Caden did some amazing research on the film. Together we determined that it is one of the earliest (and also one of the best) portrayals in world cinema of a transmasculine character. And the film’s protagonist, Bauer (the film’s title is his dead name), shines through as an incredible transmasc hero. As he confidently proclaims to the powers that be, ‘I’m not what everyone thinks I am. You hear me? I’m different. I’m something else. Something else.’” —Series curator Jenni Olson, queer film historian and archivist

An infusion of fresh blood—quite literally, in the sanguinary opening credits—for Bram Stoker’s well-thumbed tale of the macabre, by turns elegant and frightfully visceral. Along with The Curse of Frankenstein, Horror of Dracula was decisive in Hammer’s turn to Gothic horror, embraced by thrill-loving audiences around the world, though not the reviewer of the Daily Telegraph, who sniffed: “This British film has an X certificate. This is too good for it. There should be a new certificate—‘S’ for sadistic or just ‘D’ for disgusting.”

screenings.title: Ec: Hollis Frampton
screenings.description: ZORNS LEMMA(1970, 60 min, 16mm. Preserved by Anthology Film Archives.)“A major poetic work. Created and put together by a very clear eye-head, this original and complex abstract work moves beyond the letters of the alphabet, beyond words and beyond Freud. If you don’t understand it the first time you see it, don’t despair, see it again! When you finally ‘get it,’ a small light, possibly a candle, will light itself inside your forehead.” –Ernie Gehr&HAPAX LEGOMENA I: (nostalgia)(1971, 36 min, 16mm. Preserved by Anthology Film Archives, MoMA, and the NYU Moving Image Archiving and Preservation Program, with funding from the National Film Preservation Foundation.)“In (nostalgia) the time it takes for a photograph to burn (and thus confirm its two-dimensionality) becomes the clock within the film, while Frampton plays the critic, asynchronously glossing, explicating, narrating, mythologizing his earlier art, and his earlier life, as he commits them both to the fire of a labyrinthine structure; for Borges too was one of his earlier masters, and he grins behind the facades of logic, mathematics, and physical demonstrations which are the formal metaphors for most of Frampton’s films.” –P. screenings.title: The Trouble with Harry
screenings.description: The inconvenient corpse, imbued with a sense of tragedy and terror in Hitchcock’s Rope, is the source of borderline-surrealist farce in The Trouble with Harry, his adaptation of Jack Trevor Story’s novel of the same name, a darkly comic tale in which the residents of a small New England hamlet—exteriors were shot on location in Vermont, with the fall foliage radiant in Technicolor—try and repeatedly fail to dispose of a dead body that has appeared in their midst. A rare foray into comedy (albeit of the black variety) for Hitchcock, with Shirley MacLaine, Mildred Natwick, and Jerry “The Beaver” Mathers perfectly embodying a bevy of smalltown American “types.”

screenings.title: The Brides of Dracula
screenings.description: Two years after Horror of Dracula, Peter Cushing returned to the role of Doctor Van Helsing, summoned to deal with an outbreak of vampirism at a girls finishing school unleashed by a contaminated aristocrat, Baron Meinster (David Peel). Hammer’s high-finish craftsmanship is on display in every shot and in every aspect of The Brides of Dracula’s production, from Jack Asher’s baroque photography to Bernard Robinson’s exquisite set dressing to the uniformly fine work of the ensemble cast, with notable supporting turns by Martita Hunt and Yvonne Monlaur. Even without Christopher Lee, the genius of the system prevails under Fisher’s hand, giving us, per his biographer Tony Dalton, “One of those perfect Hammer ‘magic box’ productions.”

screenings.title: Poltergeist
screenings.description: Dir. Tobe Hooper. 1982, 114 mins. U.S. 35mm. With JoBeth Williams, Craig T. Nelson, Heather O’Rourke, Beatrice Straight. Melding the immense—and wildly different—talents of Tobe Hooper (The Texas Chainsaw Massacre) and Steven Spielberg (who co-wrote and produced), this haunted-house blockbuster is the ultimate suburban nightmare. After cherubic five-year-old Carol Anne Freeling is abducted by malevolent spirits, her parents are determined to bring her back at any cost. A furiously entertaining, emotionally gripping ghost story that has terrorized kids (and their parents) for 30 years, Poltergeist is a major horror spectacle that is equal parts domestic drama, dark comedy, suspense, and gross-out, featuring fantastic practical effects, from gruesomely tactile unearthed skeletons in the swimming pool to flesh-ripping hallucinations to all matter of ghostly visitors. screenings.title: Suspiria
screenings.description: Both the pinnacle of his career and the giallo subgenre, Dario Argento’s Suspiria ranks in the pantheon of the greatest horror movies of all time, and with damn good reason. Masterfully employing dream logic (the script was co-written by then wife Daria Nicolodi) and gloriously garish lighting techniques, the film is a true modern fairy tale that tells the story of a ballet student (Jessica Harper) who transfers to a German dance academy only to find it is run by a coven of murderous witches. Argento’s command of shock and suspense is on full display in every blood-soaked scene, but the true secret weapon of Suspiria is the unbelievably scary and propulsive score by the prog rock band Goblin. It all adds up to that rare witches brew: the perfect horror experience.

screenings.title: Ec: Franju / Genet
screenings.description: Georges FranjuBLOOD OF THE BEASTS / LE SANG DES BÊTES1949, 20 min, 16mm. In French with English subtitles.“This documentary on the slaughterhouses of Paris is one of the great masterpieces of the subversive cinema; here, for once, we are face to face with death, and are neither protected nor cheated. […] A dream-like quality permeates the intense realism of the images; a surrealist intent – akin to Buñuel’s slitting of the eyeball in UN CHIEN ANDALOU – is discernible in this anti-bourgeois film. But the eyeball, however shocking, was fictional; BLOOD OF THE BEASTS is real.” –Amos Vogel, FILM AS A SUBVERSIVE ARTJean GenetUN CHANT D’AMOUR1950, 26 min, 35mm, silent. Brand-new 35mm print by Anthology!“Genet’s only film – hounded by the censors, unavailable, secret – is an early and remarkably moving attempt to portray homosexual passions. Already a classic, it succeeds as perhaps no other film to intimate the explosive power of frustrated sex…. Like all Genet’s early work, the entire film is, in effect, a single onanistic fantasy, filled with desperate frustration and sensuous nostalgia.” –Amos Vogel, FILM AS A SUBVERSIVE ART“There’s no smoke without fire; UN CHANT D’AMOUR is a communion in which Genet takes us into the prison in order to liberate us from it.” –Derek JarmanTotal running time: ca. 50 min.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Halloween
screenings.description: Credited, rightfully, as the film that kickstarted the “slasher” subgenre, Carpenter’s 1978 Halloween is a masterwork of building tension, an exercise in mood and suspense that takes its cues from Hitchcock, unlike most of the 80s gorefests it would inspire. The film’s key innovation – besides the indelibly terrifying image of the blank-faced “shape” aka Michael Myers – is setting it in an innocuous American suburb; there’s nowhere, not even a nice middle class home, where the viewer is safe. Jamie Lee Curtis makes her scream queen debut as one of several babysitters being stalked by a masked, escaped mental patient on Halloween night, her only savior being the patient’s maniacally driven doctor, played with gusto by the great Donald Pleasance. But the secret weapon of Halloween is the score – composed by Carpenter himself – a tinkling, off-meter piano figure that continues to haunt long after the final unsettling frame. A Halloween season perennial.

screenings.title: Rosemary's Baby
screenings.description: “He has his father’s eyes…” Satanists are on the loose in Central Park West in Polanski’s slow-burn thriller, which slips almost imperceptibly from the quotidian into the profane, and gives new meaning to the phrase “pregnancy scare.” Young marrieds Mia Farrow and John Cassavetes make friendly with their elder neighbors Ruth Gordon and Sidney Blackmer, but when Farrow’s abandoned and isolated Rosemary goes into a paranoiac tailspin while expecting her first child, she begins to wonder why everyone is so very eager for her to take her daily dosage of tannis root… A masterclass in slow-building, spine-tingling suspense, aided immeasurably by the dab-handed work of legendary editor Sam O’Steen.

screenings.title: Blade Runner: The Final Cut
screenings.description: While so many special effects spectacles are lost in time like tears in the rain, Blade Runner remains the template for imagining the neon-wreathed downer of the future, every bit as influential in its vision as was Fritz Lang’s Metropolis over a half century before. Working from a novel by cult writer Philip K. Dick to create a film that would become the gold standard for sci-fi noir, director Scott shares credit here with “visual futurist” Syd Mead’s design concepts and synth pioneer Vangelis’s atmospheric score.

screenings.description: Fleischman took home a richly deserved Academy Award for Best Sound Mixing for his work on Scorsese’s unexpected—and thoroughly delightful—turn to family-friendly fare. A storybook tale of an orphaned 12-year-old who keeps up the clocks at Paris’s Gare Montparnasse following his father’s death who, through a serendipitous encounter with aged, forgotten filmmaker Georges Méliès (Ben Kingsley), finds a new makeshift family through his immersion in the world of cinema. From the pulsing sounds of the busy train station to the bravura nightmare sequence in which a locomotive smashes through the station’s walls, Fleischman’s marvelously detailed soundscapes give Scorsese’s pre-war Paris period piece an immediate thrumming vitality.

screenings.title: Hocus Pocus

After dismissing a story Allison tells as superstitious, Max accidentally frees a coven of evil witches who used to live in the house. Now, with the help of a magical cat, the kids must steal the witches’ book of spells to stop them from becoming immortal.

screenings.description: Among the most perfectly cast Hollywood studio films of the last half-century, cinematographer-cum-director Sonnenfeld’s adaptation of Charles Addams’s macabre recurring New Yorker feature stars Raul Julia as the suave patriarch of the Addams clan (“You lady-killer…” “Acquitted!”), Anjelica Huston as his waxen, witchy bride, and an outstanding preadolescent Christina Ricci as doomy daughter Wednesday. A drolly dark comedy that moves with the fearsome speed of a 1930s screwball, thanks to the surgical precision of Dede Allen’s editing.

screenings.title: Cat People (1942)
screenings.description: Irena Dubrovna (Simone Simon), a New York City–based fashion designer who hails from Serbia, begins a romance with marine engineer Oliver Reed (Kent Smith). After the couple gets married, Oliver becomes concerned about Irena’s notion that she is cursed and may transform into a large cat in the heat of passion. Confiding in his beautiful assistant, Alice Moore (Jane Randolph), about his marital issues, Oliver unwittingly triggers Irena’s curse, with tragic results.

screenings.title: The Shining: International Version (U.S. Theatrical Premiere) with Garrett Brown and Michael Chaiken in person
screenings.description: Preceded by a conversation with Steadicam inventor Garrett Brown and archivist Michael Chaiken Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1980. 114 mins. U.S. 4K DCP. With Jack Nicholson, Shelley Duvall, Scatman Crothers, Danny Loyd. When The Shining was first released in 1980, most critics were generally baffled or negative, unable to understand Stanley Kubrick’s visionary approach to the horror genre, which prioritized deliberate pacing, deferred catharsis, and haunting abstract imagery. Today, we see, of course, that Kubrick was laying the groundwork for future generations of aspiring art-horror filmmakers. But in the moment, Kubrick responded to the critiques by editing a shorter version with less slack for the European market, a tinkered cut that he called “The Two-Hour Version.” Shining obsessive and Pixar animator Lee Unkrich—writer of the Taschen book Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining—notes that Kubrick’s long-time assistant Leon Vitali claimed this was Kubrick’s preferred cut. Decide for yourself in this rare opportunity to see the International Version on the big screen, followed by a screening of the original U.S. cut. screenings.title: Wild at Heart (new Restoration)
screenings.description: After serving prison time for a self-defense killing, Sailor Ripley (Nicolas Cage) reunites with girlfriend Lula Fortune (Laura Dern). Lula's mother, Marietta (Diane Ladd), desperate to keep them apart, hires a hit man to kill Sailor. But he finds a whole new set of troubles when he and Bobby Peru (Willem Dafoe), an old buddy who's also out to get Sailor, try to rob a store. When Sailor lands in jail yet again, the young lovers appear further than ever from the shared life they covet.

screenings.title: All That Heaven Allows
screenings.description: Perhaps the very finest of Sirk’s Ross Hunter-produced melodramas, All That Heaven Allows pairs Jane Wyman and Rock Hudson as, respectively, a well-off widow in country club Connecticut, and the broad-necked, Thoreau-reading gardener who she falls for. Her priggish children, aghast, conspire to break off the pairing, an endeavor that ends in a bone-chilling Christmas conciliation—the presentation of a gift television set as a kind of death sentence. Of this scene Rainer Werner Fassbinder, profoundly marked by his encounter with Sirk’s film, would write: “At that point everyone in the moviehouse breaks down. They suddenly understand something about the world and what it does to people.” Right on.

screenings.title: Sans Soleil
screenings.description: Marker's voyage through memory, history, and video games is a free-flow of images shot largely in Japan (a cat temple, sacred phalluses, horror movies, sleeping subway riders, an animatronic JFK), with detours to Guinea-Bissau, Iceland, and, for an extended homage to Vertigo, San Francisco. An alien travelog? The world’s most profound home movie? There’s nothing quite like it in the history of cinema.

screenings.title: Freaked | The Surreal Nightmares of Screaming Mad George
screenings.description: One of the quintessential early-’90s cult films, Freaked was adapted by Alex Winter and Tom Stern from their psychotronic MTV series The Idiot Box. Winter plays a vain Hollywood actor who takes a gig promoting an evil South African fertilizer company. But an airplane incident lands him in the middle of a grotesque amusement park, where he is transformed into a member of its expansive freak show. A deliriously grotesque live-action cartoon, Freaked is a carnivalesque melange of eye-popping make-up effects and fun-house set design. It also features an all-star cameo casting ranging from Gibby Haynes of The Butthole Surfers to Mr. T, plus masked appearances from Keanu Reeves and future Wicked director Jon M. Chu. Must be seen to be believed.

screenings.title: Occupational Hazard: the First Coral Reefers
screenings.description: OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD: THE FIRST CORAL REEFERS is a feature documentary that journeys back to the 1970s and early 1980s to tell the story of Jimmy Buffett’s original Coral Reefer Band. Set against the creative backdrop of Key West, the film explores the musicians, friendships, touring years, and studio sessions that helped shape Buffett’s legendary sound. Through rare, never-before-seen archival footage and deeply personal interviews with founding members, tour managers, producers and music legends, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD captures the camaraderie, chaos, and magic of an era that thrived on freedom and lived without a rulebook. Narrated by Academy-award winner Jeff Bridges, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD offers fans a deeper look at the people behind the music and the era that helped define Jimmy Buffett’s lasting legacy. This film is a tribute to Buffett and the original Coral Reefers, the places and people that shaped them, the volatile beauty of a musical moment that couldn’t last but changed everything and their candid sentiment toward Buffett. It’s the origin story upon which the Parrot Head empire was built upon, by the people who helped lay the foundation.

screenings.description: In their tireless search for new monsters to add to their menagerie Hammer turned here to Greek mythology, unleashing the fatal gaze of the Gorgon on the residents of a German village, c. 1910. Seven Vandorf residents have in recent years been found frozen into statuary, and it falls on the esteemed Prof. Meister of Leipzig (Christopher Lee) to overcome interference by local physician Dr. Namaroff (Peter Cushing) and track down the culprit, Megaera (ballerina-turned-film actor Prudence Hyman), a she-devil with the ability to turn flesh to stone. A small miracle of high style on a pinched budget, praised by Raymond Durgnat in Films and Filming for its “romantic warmth… with oil lamps casting a rich glow on the patchwork counterpanes and through coloured windows, and with some extraordinarily beautiful cloudscapes and dusk skies.”

screenings.title: Manhood
screenings.description: MANHOOD follows Dallas entrepreneur Bill Moore as he attempts to make penis enlargement as commonplace as Botox. Along the way, an OnlyFans star and a father of five put their bodies — and their insecurities — on the line. screenings.title: Ec: Ernie Gehr
screenings.description: “Ernie Gehr [makes] cinematic magic, often from the least likely materials. Indeed, Gehr’s most famous film, SERENE VELOCITY (1970), in which the filmmaker transforms an institutional hallway in the basement of a classroom building at the State University of New York at Binghamton into a nexus of visual and conceptual energy, merely by adjusting his stationary camera’s zoom lens every four frames for twenty-three minutes, can be read as Gehr’s manifesto. For Gehr the most everyday spaces and the most mundane actions offer the imaginative filmmaker the most interesting potential. No other filmmaker, with the exception of Michael Snow, has so relentlessly and so productively explored the capacity of filmmaking to develop the visual (and auditory) opportunities afforded by the cinematic apparatus itself.” –Scott MacDonald, A CRITICAL CINEMA 5REVERBERATION (1969, 23 min, 16mm)SERENE VELOCITY (1970, 23 min, 16mm, silent)&STILL1971, 54 min, 16mm. screenings.title: Ganja & Hess | Bill Gunn at Roxy!
screenings.description: Flirting with the conventions of blaxploitation and horror, Bill Gunn’s revolutionary independent film Ganja & Hess is a highly stylized and utterly original treatise on sex, religion, and African American identity. Duane Jones (Night of the Living Dead) stars as anthropologist Hess Green, who is stabbed with an ancient ceremonial dagger by his unstable assistant (director Bill Gunn), bestowing upon him the blessing of immortality… and the curse of an unquenchable thirst for blood. When the assistant’s beautiful and outspoken wife Ganja (Marlene Clark) comes searching for her missing husband, she and Hess form an unexpected partnership. Together, they explore just how much power blood holds.

screenings.title: Who Killed Alex Odeh?
screenings.description: In October 1985, Santa Ana, California was shaken by a brazen act of political violence when Palestinian American Alex Odeh, a beloved teacher and community leader, was killed by a tripwire bomb planted in his office. Despite substantial evidence and identified suspects, the case was never solved. Who Killed Alex Odeh? reopens the mystery, tracking a renewed investigation in real time as new leads emerge, long-buried records come to light, and the forces behind a political assassination are finally confronted. In English, Arabic and Hebrew with English subtitles.

screenings.title: News from Home + Interior NY Subway, 14th Street
screenings.description: Akerman was 26 years old and living in New York City, away from her native Belgium and her mother, when she teamed with DP Babette Mangolte to film this diary/essay/poem in subway stations and on street corners, their images to eventually be paired with Akerman’s recitals of her mother’s fretful letters. Arguably this extraordinary filmmaker’s most perfect and poignant nonfiction work, both one of the greatest portraits of a city ever put on film and a troubling, touching depiction of maternal love. Screens in the English-language version.

screenings.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
screenings.description: An ardent aficionado of the work of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, Cushing takes over the chambers at 221B Baker Street with aplomb and gives us a Sherlock for the ages in Fisher’s adaptation of the 1902 Holmes adventure of the same name, in which our hero is called to Dartmoor to investigate the mysterious death-by-fright of one Sir Charles Baskerville, leaving his estate in the hands of his heir and nephew, Henry (Christopher Lee). With the invaluable assistance of Jack Asher’s subdued Technicolor photography, Fisher wrings every drop of atmosphere out of Doyle’s tale of mist-shrouded moors and ancestral curses, making this one of Holmes’s very finest big-screen outings. (Special mention is due to Fisher’s ingenious use of child stand-ins for his leads to establish the terrible proportions of the eponymous mastiff.)

screenings.description: The series curator’s dark horse pick for must-see movie in the Screaming Mad George retrospective, the late entry from the direct-to-video years of the long, byzantine Christmas series is shockingly entertaining. The story involves a young boy who is traumatized when bizarre mystery toys kill people including his deadbeat father, his school bully, and a landlord (yes!) in strange and gruesome ways. This puts him in touch with a toy seller named Joe Petto—owner of “Petto’s Toys” (say it out loud)—played by a typically unhinged late-career Mickey Rooney. And from there, the story takes a twist into being a… Terminator knock-off? To the best of our knowledge, Silent Night, Deadly Night 5: The Toy Maker has never screened theatrically in New York City on 35mm.

screenings.title: Something Special (Willy/Milly)
screenings.description: Frustrated by a world in which boys seem to get the best of everything, 14-year-old Milly (Pamela Adlon) makes a wish to swap her sex, and wakes up to find her—or, rather, his—wish has come true. “In my obsession with Something Special, I purchased this 35mm print of it almost 30 years ago. There are a handful of ‘teenage girls passing as boys’ films (She’s the Man is probably the best known). In so many films with gender-crossing characters, the passing is so unconvincing that it renders the film ultimately unsatisfying for a queer audience. But Pamela Adlon’s performance here as Willy is absolutely spectacular.” —Series curator Jenni Olson, queer film historian and archivist

screenings.title: Rushmore
screenings.description: Extracurricular-mad but otherwise unpromising 15-year-old student Max Fisher (Jason Schwartzman) is too busy competing (or so he thinks) with sad sack industrialist Bill Murray for the affections of teacher Olivia Williams to survive “sudden death academic probation” in Anderson’s deeply funny, deeply melancholic—and very class-conscious—sophomore feature. A back-to-school perennial, all dressed up in prep school navy blue and the muted colors of north Texas autumn, positively thrumming with the upstart energy of British Invasion anthems. (“Anderson,” noted admirer Martin Scorsese, “has a fine sense of how music works against an image.”) An irresistible, disarmingly original, delicately wrought comic fable.

screenings.title: Autumn Sonata
screenings.description: Ingmar and Ingrid, Bergman and Bergman, together at last. Sweden’s most popular export before the Volvo, in her final screen role, plays a world-renowned concert pianist who returns home to reunite with her now-married daughter (Liv Ullmann), long a distant second to her mother’s career ambitions, the two women exhuming old resentments and struggling towards reconciliation over the course of an emotionally draining 24 hours. “So unrelenting, so harrowing, that I walked out of the theater on shaking legs. If you’re open to the experience that Bergman means to provide, you may leave the film muttering a wrung-out ‘Whew!’ followed quickly by an appreciative ‘Wow!’” —Richard Corliss, Time Magazine

screenings.title: Midnight in Paris
screenings.description: Screenwriter, would-be novelist, and romantic-at-heart Owen Wilson, on vacation in the City of Lights with level-headed fiancée Rachel McAdams, sets out on his own one night after a wine tasting and finds himself suddenly in the Jazz Age Paris of Fitzgerald and Hemingway, Dali and Picasso—an invigorating draught of bohemian freedom that sets our protagonist to seriously interrogating his life choices. “We talked about pushing the color even more in the period scenes, in order to distinguish them from the present-day ones. The Paris of today would be normal and generic, bland and desaturated, and when you entered the Paris of the 1920s the colors would be more warm, lush and flamboyant, with lots of brown and gold and red.” —Darius Khondji

screenings.title: Occupational Hazard: the First Coral Reefers
screenings.description: OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD: THE FIRST CORAL REEFERS is a feature documentary that journeys back to the 1970s and early 1980s to tell the story of Jimmy Buffett’s original Coral Reefer Band. Set against the creative backdrop of Key West, the film explores the musicians, friendships, touring years, and studio sessions that helped shape Buffett’s legendary sound. Through rare, never-before-seen archival footage and deeply personal interviews with founding members, tour managers, producers and music legends, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD captures the camaraderie, chaos, and magic of an era that thrived on freedom and lived without a rulebook. Narrated by Academy-award winner Jeff Bridges, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD offers fans a deeper look at the people behind the music and the era that helped define Jimmy Buffett’s lasting legacy. This film is a tribute to Buffett and the original Coral Reefers, the places and people that shaped them, the volatile beauty of a musical moment that couldn’t last but changed everything and their candid sentiment toward Buffett. It’s the origin story upon which the Parrot Head empire was built upon, by the people who helped lay the foundation.

screenings.title: Bride of Re-Animator | The Surreal Nightmares of Screaming Mad George
screenings.description: The original Re-Animator adapted Frankenstein-by-way-of-Lovecraft into a bloodsoaked med school nightmare. And like any great sequel, Bride of Re-Animator goes bigger, zanier, and gorier, with moments that represent the zenith of practical effects work. Reuniting stars Jeffrey Combs as Dr. Herbert West and Bruce Abbott as former medical student Dr. Dan Cain, Bride sees the duo expand their experiments to re-animating individual severed limbs. Their goal: to resurrect Cain’s fiance by cobbling pieces of other women around her preserved heart. And from there, the creations only get crazier. Bride of Re-Animator is an extraordinary follow-up to Brian Yuzna and Screaming Mad George’s previous collaboration Society with an all-star special effects team also includes John Carl Buechler and the KNB EFX Group.

screenings.description: Kurt Russell is Jack Burton, an independent trucker piloting the Pork Chop Express through the streets of San Francisco’s Chinatown. When a new friend’s fiancée is kidnapped, the pair find themselves thrust into the middle of a supernatural gang war that pits them against dueling sorcerers, freakish fiends, and black magic. Big Trouble in Little China combines John Carpenter’s affinity for burly men-on-a-mission narratives with the fantastical tropes of vintage adventure serials—an even more colorful, cartoonish, and muscular take on the Indiana Jones formula. The follow-up to this authentic document of youth culture was the ZDF production BORED TEENAGERS, part of the “Das kleine Fernsehspiel” series; it was filmed in 1979 in the wake of the RAF panic – wanted posters are visible in the background several times throughout the film. The movie blends concert footage of the English punk band The Adverts with a loose narrative thread about a young punk named Peter and his hairdresser girlfriend, Karin, as they follow the band – led by TV Smith and Gaye Advert – on their tour through Germany. screenings.title: Occupational Hazard: the First Coral Reefers
screenings.description: OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD: THE FIRST CORAL REEFERS is a feature documentary that journeys back to the 1970s and early 1980s to tell the story of Jimmy Buffett’s original Coral Reefer Band. Set against the creative backdrop of Key West, the film explores the musicians, friendships, touring years, and studio sessions that helped shape Buffett’s legendary sound. Through rare, never-before-seen archival footage and deeply personal interviews with founding members, tour managers, producers and music legends, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD captures the camaraderie, chaos, and magic of an era that thrived on freedom and lived without a rulebook. Narrated by Academy-award winner Jeff Bridges, OCCUPATIONAL HAZARD offers fans a deeper look at the people behind the music and the era that helped define Jimmy Buffett’s lasting legacy. This film is a tribute to Buffett and the original Coral Reefers, the places and people that shaped them, the volatile beauty of a musical moment that couldn’t last but changed everything and their candid sentiment toward Buffett. It’s the origin story upon which the Parrot Head empire was built upon, by the people who helped lay the foundation.

screenings.title: Visible Humans
screenings.description: With artist and ophthalmologist Benjamin Freeman and curator Elisabeth Sherman in person The Visible Human Project began in the late 1990s with sponsorship from the National Library of Medicine. Its aim was to make a complete 3D rendering of the human body for educational use. Now in the public domain, these images raise questions about consent and normative ideals. This evening will interrogate this project and feature a screening of the short film Visible Woman, which is included in our exhibition Overexposed; a presentation by ophthalmologist and photographer Benjamin Freeman; and a discussion including curator Elisabeth Sherman. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission. Special Guests: Elisabeth Sherman is the Robert A. and Elizabeth Rohn Jeffe Chief Curator and Deputy Director at the Museum of the City of New York. Previously, she was Chief Curator and Director of Curatorial Affairs at the International Center of Photography (ICP). Prior to ICP, she was a curator at the Whitney Museum of American Art, where she organized and co-organized many critically acclaimed exhibitions including Dawoud Bey: An American Project, Zoe Leonard: Survey, and Making Knowing: Craft in Art, 1960-2019. At ICP she curated, among others, Naima Green: Instead, I Spin Fantasies, Sheida Soleimani: Panjereh, Yto Barrada: Part Time Abstractionist, and ICP at 50. She is co-editor of the catalog Overexposed: Art, Technology, and the Body. Benji Freeman is a photographer and physician based in New York City. His photography draws from medical epistemologies, techniques, and image archives, investigating the modern aesthetics of caring for others as the actual work of healthcare becomes increasingly automatable. He has taught workshops on photographic technique, the visual culture of medicine, and the anatomy of the visual system, and he has written about the role of photographic perception in medical education. He is currently an ophthalmology resident at Columbia University Medical Center.

screenings.title: The Draughtsman's Contract + Live Performance | Instruments of Desire
screenings.description: Set in a richly exaggerated 17th-century England, Peter Greenaway’s sumptuous and sensuously charged brainteaser catapulted him to the forefront of international art cinema. Adorned with intricate wordplay, extravagant costumes and opulent photography, Greenaway’s first narrative feature weaves a labyrinthine mystery around the maxim “draw what you see, not what you know.” An aristocratic wife (Janet Suzman) commissions a young, cocksure draughtsman (Anthony Higgins) to sketch her husband’s property while he is away—in exchange for a fee, room and board, and one sexual favor for each of the twelve drawings. As the draughtsman becomes more entrenched in the devious schemings in this seemingly idyllic country home, curious details emerge in his drawings that may reveal a murder.

screenings.title: Last Stop for the Circular Ticket
screenings.description: THE THEATER OF THE MATTERS & TAUFIC PRESENT:JEAN-CLAUDE ROUSSEAU’S ‘THE PASTORAL CONCERT’ + ‘LAST STOP FOR THE CIRCULAR TICKET’This book launch event celebrates the release of Jean-Claude Rousseau’s unclassifiable, long-unavailable film text, The Pastoral Concert, published for the first time in English this October by Taufic. The evening will culminate in a special premiere screening of Rousseau’s new feature film, LAST STOP FOR THE CIRCULAR TICKET (winner of a Jury Special Mention at this year’s FIDMarseille), alongside his 2006 short, FAUX DÉPART.The Pastoral Concert marks the first English translation of Rousseau’s early written work Le Concert champêtre, begun in 1968, some fifteen years before his debut film. Rousseau continued shaping the work as a screenplay until its rejection by the Centre National de la Cinématographie in 1983. Unrealized, Le Concert champêtre became the matrix from which Rousseau’s subsequent films would emerge.Taking its title and three central characters (A, B, and C) from the eponymous painting long attributed to Giorgione and now to Titian, The Pastoral Concert begins as a letter written by a young man to his cousin in the countryside on the eve of her wedding, before mutating into a diary entry, a screenplay, and finally a film imagined through the failure of its own realization. In this restless fluctuation between registers, The Pastoral Concert expresses, in the words of Jean-Marie Straub, “something magnificent [and] entirely different from a screenplay or a découpage.”Translated from the French by artist and filmmaker Kevin Weil, this edition includes an extensive appendix of extra-diegetic materials written by Rousseau, as well as correspondence with contemporaries such as Dominique Noguez, Marcel Hanoun, and Jean-Marie Straub, which form a picture of the work’s early reception.For more info about The Pastoral Concert visit: https://taufic.org/the-pastoral-concertJean-Claude RousseauLAST STOP FOR THE CIRCULAR TICKET / DERNIER ARRÊT POUR LE BILLET CIRCULAIRE2026, 87 min, DCP. No dialogue.Rousseau’s longest film since THE ENCLOSED VALLEY from 1995 (the summit of his 8mm era), LAST STOP FOR THE CIRCULAR TICKET refers to the looped ferry route that plies the waters of Lake Como in Northern Italy. Firmly grounded in place, Rousseau’s solitary camera finds desolate poetry in the void of the spectacular landscape and in the anonymous crowds of passengers seemingly entranced at the edge of an abyss. Musical chords and voices magnify their gestures and the movement of the vessel on the lake. Closing the circle, the specter of the end looms: “On the ferry, among the travelers, I recognized Mrs. Death…”Preceded by:Jean-Claude Rousseau FAUX DÉPART (2006, 13 min, DCP. Winner of the Golden Leopard at last year’s Locarno Film Festival, hailed “a true masterpiece” by Shiguéhiko Hasumi, Japan’s greatest living film critic, Two Seasons, Two Strangers is at one and the same time as simple as its straightforward title suggests and immensely, exhilaratingly complex. Preceded by Miyake’s short Nagahama, born of a creative collaboration with dancer and actress Shizuka Ishibashi.

screenings.description: EMBODIED TECHNOLOGY With directors Kogonada and Noam Argov in person After Yang. Dir. Kogonada. 2022, 96 mins. With Colin Farrell, Justin H. Min, Jodie Turner-Smith, Haley Lu Richardson, Malea Emma Tjandrawidjaja. When his young daughter’s technosapien companion, the android Yang (Min), malfunctions, Jake (Farrell) must come to terms with what this loss means for his family. Adapted from a short story by Alexander Weinstein, and directed with aesthetic precision and restraint by Kogonada, the director of tender films about interpersonal connection such as Columbus and this year’s Zi, After Yang is a sensitive and visually striking inquiry into what it means to be human. Preceded by Verse. Dir. Noam Argov. 2026, 18 mins. With Taj Cross, Jesse LaTourette, Will Dagger. Seventeen-year-old Adam is forced to confront where his virtual persona ends and his physical self begins when he decides to meet his VR girlfriend in real life. Both of these films have received recognition and/or support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation’s program in Public Understanding of Science and Technology. His first feature, Columbus, premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017. Noam Argov is an award-winning writer/director and National Geographic Explorer whose work explores identity and the spaces between worlds. Her 2023 narrative short Sulam (Ladder) premiered in competition at Aspen Shortsfest and won Best U.S. Student Film at Palm Springs ShortFest; her feature screenplay Princess won NYU’s Purple List Table-Read Initiative, where it was staged in its entirety for producers and executives; and her latest short, Verse, received the Sloan Production Award for its exploration of VR and neuroscience and had its world premiere at the 2026 Tribeca Film Festival. Noam is also a producer on Forbidden Fruits (SXSW 2026), starring Lili Reinhart and Lola Tung and released theatrically by IFC, and Punter, a proof-of-concept film executive produced by Spike Lee and a finalist for the Student BAFTA. Sappir Argov is an American actor and writer whose work spans film, podcasting, and live performance. She is a co-writer of Verse. Sappir starred in short films for top-tier MFA programs, including NYU Tisch and UCLA, as well as an independent short screened for producers at Blumhouse. She is also starring in two upcoming projects slated for release in 2026. Her commercial work includes a global travel campaign aired on NBC. In her writing, Sappir’s original podcast Passing Through ranked in the Top 100 narrative comedy shows on Apple Podcasts.

screenings.title: Personal Problems | Bill Gunn at Roxy!
screenings.description: What happens when a group of unbankable individuals tell their stories? Actors who have final say over their speaking parts? A director who was found ‘too difficult’ for Hollywood? A composer who would not submit the hack soundtracks required by the industry? A Black male lead who was not Black enough? A Black actress who was not light enough? An actor who had been retired because he belonged to another era? A cinematographer who chose art over expediency? An unmarketable co-actor who didn’t look like Clark Gable or a male version of Vanessa Williams? Two producers, having no experience, had the audacity to organize a production with the amount of money that Hollywood spends on catering? Maybe less.

screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. screenings.title: Asako I & II
screenings.description: Following up Happy Hour, his justly acclaimed epic of everyday life, Hamaguchi offers a different but no less quietly revolutionary vision with this pop romance that moves from youthful exuberance and delusion to mature circumspection and compromise, while keeping up throughout a magical tonal balance of wistfulness, comic buoyancy, and the ineffably heartbreaking. As a student in Osaka, Asako meets and falls in love with a drifter named Baku who one day drifts right out of her life. Two years later, working in Tokyo, she sees Baku again—or, rather, a young, solid businessman named Ryohei who is Baku’s double in every respect save personality. After initial astonishment, they begin to build a life together—but a twist in circumstances threatens to tear it all down, and forces Asako to confront her long, lingering love affair with a half-ghost fantasy.

screenings.title: The Woman in the Window
screenings.description: Alone for the holiday while his wife and children are on vacation, the staid, middle-aged college professor Richard Wanley (Edward G. Robinson) is about to settle in to an uneventful stretch of nights spent sipping port by the fireplace of his club—but then he catches a glimpse of a beguiling brunette in a gallery window and, in short order, finds himself having a drink with the model (Joan Bennett), after which everything goes straight to hell. Involved in a self-defense killing and its subsequent cover-up, Wanley finds himself investigating his own crime at the elbow of fellow clubman and D.A. Frank Lalor (Raymond Massey), the noose tightening around his neck with the emergence of every fresh clue and misstep. A high-style turning-of-the-screws noir suspenser, with a wonderfully oleaginous turn from heel extraordinaire Dan Duryea.

screenings.title: Tenebrae
screenings.description: Argento’s return to his giallo roots after veering off into gonzo horror/fantasy, Tenebrae features Anthony Franciosa as an American author of potboiler thrillers who, promoting a new book in Rome, finds that a murderer is re-enacting his most ghoulish delights of literary fancy. Argento uses the occasion to scale new, dizzying heights of his own, employing bravura crane shots, brazenly baroque lighting, and the iconic moment of a razor slashing through white cotton.

screenings.title: The Brood
screenings.description: In The Brood, the bitter divorce between the mentally disturbed Nola (Samantha Eggar) and her ex-husband Frank (Art Hindle) was pretty messy, so it should be a good sign that she’s finally getting professional help from the renowned Dr. Hal Raglan (Oliver Reed)—but Frank can’t help but notice that people on Nola’s long list of enemies keep dying at the hands of asexual, dwarfish assassins, and so he starts to wonder what exactly the experimental therapy practiced at Dr. Raglan’s Somafree Institute consists of… Written while Cronenberg was in the midst of his own divorce and custody battle, The Brood is a brutal, bracing airing of anxieties gussied up in grindhouse trappings.

screenings.title: Spellbound
screenings.description: Hitchcock goes in for psychoanalysis in this singular thriller, made under the influence of Sigmund Freud and Salvador Dalí, the latter of whom designed the dazzling dream sequence. Analyst Ingrid Bergman falls for amnesiac patient Gregory Peck—but is there a murderer’s heart lurking beneath that dapper exterior? The delirium only grows more intense and Miklós Rózsa’s theremin-inflected score becomes more urgent as her doubts grow and she draws closer to the truth.

screenings.title: The General
screenings.description: Keaton’s engineer Johnnie Gray is another of his big-hearted little guys, rejected by the Confederate Army, though when the Union tries to make off with his train, runt Johnnie shows his mettle in the most incredible sustained chase sequence in all of silent comedy. Wall-to-wall with elaborate, antic gags, though also marked by a quiet sense of pastoral beauty that had previously been given little outlet.

screenings.title: The Killing
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1956. 85 mins. 35mm. With Sterling Hayden, Coleen Gray, Vince Edwards, Jay C. Flippen, Elisha Cook Jr., Marie Windsor. Stanley Kubrick and pulp-fiction legend Jim Thompson co-wrote this darkly comic thriller about a racetrack heist gone awry. With its thick layers of irony and stopwatch-precise playing with time, Kubrick’s fragmented crime noir (whose existential overtones and intricate structure inspired Quentin Tarantino’s Reservoir Dogs) is his true narrative breakthrough, laying the groundwork for a filmography of flawed, failed masculinity and fatalistic humor. screenings.description: Camila (Agustina Muñoz), a young Argentine theater director, travels from Buenos Aires to New York for an artistic residency where she intends to develop her new project: a new Spanish translation of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream—but upon her arrival, Camila quickly realizes that her work isn’t compensating for the loss of her friends and boyfriend she left behind. A film of quiet passion in which small gestures and objects carry great emotional weight, Hermia & Helena was the first film Piñeiro made in his adoptive home of New York City, released 10 years ago, and as such is ideally suited to screen alongside the stateside launch of his new artist’s book from Fireflies Press, From where do you start when drawing a flower?

screenings.title: The Battle of Tuntenhaus
screenings.description: Juliet BashoreTHE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 1 1991, 24 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.THE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 2 1992, 19 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Suzhou River
screenings.description: Taking its name from the polluted river that flows through Shanghai, director Lou’s hometown, the brooding Suzhou River uses the singular first-person perspective of its unseen videographer-narrator to explore the grubby underbelly of the city, observing the story of an unsuspecting motorcycle courier who finds himself snared in a kidnapping plot and murder rap. A seductive, intricately structured stylistic coup from the Sixth Generation filmmaker, drawing on influences from film noir to Vertigo (1958) while developing its own idiosyncratic and haunting visual vocabulary.

screenings.title: Columbus
screenings.description: Modern architecture acts as a vehicle for emotional expression in Kogonada’s lauded first feature, whose title refers to the Indiana city that, thanks to the patronage of Cummins diesel engines company cofounder J. Irwin Miller, has commissioned buildings from master builders including I.M. Pei, Eero Saarinen, and Robert Venturi. A Korean American translator (John Cho) arrives in this curious testing ground for advanced architecture after his estranged scholar father falls ill, there to cross paths with dad’s protégée (Parker Posey), an aesthete clerk at the local library (Haley Lu Richardson), and a bevy of singular structures. A film of rich colors and muted yearning, and one of the most distinctive debuts in the last decade of American independent cinema.

screenings.title: The Gorgon
screenings.description: In their tireless search for new monsters to add to their menagerie Hammer turned here to Greek mythology, unleashing the fatal gaze of the Gorgon on the residents of a German village, c. 1910. Seven Vandorf residents have in recent years been found frozen into statuary, and it falls on the esteemed Prof. Meister of Leipzig (Christopher Lee) to overcome interference by local physician Dr. Namaroff (Peter Cushing) and track down the culprit, Megaera (ballerina-turned-film actor Prudence Hyman), a she-devil with the ability to turn flesh to stone. A small miracle of high style on a pinched budget, praised by Raymond Durgnat in Films and Filming for its “romantic warmth… with oil lamps casting a rich glow on the patchwork counterpanes and through coloured windows, and with some extraordinarily beautiful cloudscapes and dusk skies.”

screenings.title: zi
screenings.description: “Poetic, political, and above all incontrovertibly material” [The New Yorker], Kogonada’s fourth feature, the experimental drama zi, follows the title character, played by Michelle Mao, a concert violinist whose aimless peregrinations through the streets of Hong Kong are interrupted by visions of what may be either her past or future, a condition she attempts to explain to a new American acquaintance (Haley Lu Richardson, Columbus) while a stranger (Jin Ha) observes the pair from a distance. A valentine to the textures and colors of the Fragrant Harbor as seen by night, featuring music by the late Ryuichi Sakamoto, the formally audacious, shot-on-the-fly zi is a film of unusual delicacy and reserve, one whose air of mystery abides long after the credits have rolled.

screenings.title: Crystal Voyager
screenings.description: Directed by Elfick, co-founder of the Australian surf magazine Tracks, “the Citizen Kane of surfing pictures” [The Guardian] follows photographer, filmmaker, and avid surfer George Greenough, as well as fellow wave-chasers Nat Young and Richie West, on a quest for secluded surf spots that goes from coastal California to Lennox Head, New South Wales, to points even further afield. A heady paean to the elements, to sun and water, whose fisheye tube-riding POV shots were received as nothing short of revolutionary when it premiered, and whose psychedelic soundtrack by The Crystal Voyager Band won it an ardent following in counterculture hot spots the world over.

screenings.title: Tripolar the Movie + Q&A
screenings.description: TRIPOLAR THE MOVIE is a biting satire disguised as a stoner comedy set in the heart of Brooklyn. Rife with John Waters-style humor, the story follows a washed-up 50-something mother and her daughter’s 20-something friends who are willing to do anything to make a film. But when a movie exec greenlights their project, they begin to conspire against one another in a parody of life in modern America.

screenings.title: Nina Hagen = Punk + Glory
screenings.description: Up until his untimely death earlier this year, filmmaker Peter Sempel had a long and close association with Anthology Film Archives and Jonas Mekas (about whom he made four separate feature-length film portraits over the years). In addition to his collaborations with Jonas, Sempel made numerous other experimental films and documentaries about various artists and musicians. Among his best-known works is this film about the legendary singer, songwriter, and actress Nina Hagen. Far from a conventional artist doc, NINA HAGEN = PUNK + GLORY favors spontaneous, fragmentary, and often home-movie-like glimpses of her daily life, performances, and interactions with family, friends, and colleagues (including Lemmy, George Clinton, Blixa Bargeld, Udo Kier, Dee Dee Ramone, Jonas Mekas, and others). Sempel’s goal is less to narrate Hagen’s biography than to capture her unique energy and charisma, and to shed light on her many sides, on- and off-stage.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Sad Vacation
screenings.description: The third and final film of Aoyama’s “Kitakyushu Saga,” adapted from his own novel, stars Tadanobu Asano as Kenji, a young man still nursing the wounds of an unhappy childhood as he goes through the desultory motions of various odd jobs, who catches sight of an opportunity for closure—or, perhaps, revenge—when one night he recognizes the wife of one of his employers as the mother who’d abandoned him years ago, and conspires to infiltrate their household. A rich, moving human drama of families arbitrarily assigned and chosen, its large ensemble cast handled adroitly, and the proceedings given a striking, somber beauty by prodigiously gifted cinematographer Masaki Tamura.

screenings.title: Lost Highway
screenings.description: Few filmmakers have shown themselves so adept at plumbing the depths of the subconscious without coming up for air as Lynch, whose Lost Highway—inspired loosely by still-fresh coverage of the O. J. Simpson trial—begins as a dark domestic drama concerning a sexually incompetent saxophonist (Bill Pullman) and his wife (Patricia Arquette), morphs into a movie about a cocksman mechanic (Balthazar Getty) who gets involved with a gangster’s girl (Arquette, again), and ends with an unleashing of apocalyptic, purgative flame… Whether you take it as a cinematic depiction of a psychogenic fugue state or a free-associative disgorging of images from Hollywood’s id, Lynch’s film has the pull of a whirlpool and the terrible logic of a nightmare.

screenings.title: White Snail
screenings.description: NEW YORK PREMIERE! FILMMAKERS IN PERSON!“Following two unconventional documentaries – SPACE DOGS (2019) and DREAMING DOGS (2024) – focused on the lives of stray canines, filmmaking duo Elsa Kremser and Levin Peter return with the narrative feature WHITE SNAIL, where the two protagonists also exhibit a fondness for various animals. Set in contemporary Belarus, the film tells the story of Masha, a blonde, thin, fair-skinned model pursuing her dream job in China, and Misha, a tattooed, thickset painter working at a morgue. Played with extreme naturalness by non-professionals Marya Imbro and Mikhail Senkov, these two loners strike up an unlikely but profound friendship that will force them to confront their secrets and wounds. The worlds to which Masha and Misha belong are completely at odds. But as these characters form a strange bond, the fashion industry and the funeral business reveal equally unlikely coincidences and areas of overlap that subtly proliferate as the plot advances. By depicting how we and our bodies relate to sight and touch, life and death, reality and imagination, flaws and perfection, Kremser and Peter map two universes on to one another, leaving the viewer to determine where they intersect and whether they diverge.” –Cristina Álvarez López, VIENNALEThese screenings are co-presented by Deutsches Haus at NYU and Erste Bank, on the occasion of the co-awarding of the 2025 Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to WHITE SNAIL. Since 2011, each annual edition of the Viennale (Vienna International FilmFestival) has featured the granting of the Viennale Erste Bank Film Award to one or more filmmakers whose films are included within the festival. Designed to showcase the best of Austrian cinema, the Award was founded by Erste Bank, the Viennale’s main sponsor, and is awarded according to the findings of an independent jury. The Award brings a cash prize as well as a residency as a visiting filmmaker organized by Deutsches Haus at NYU. Additional support for these screenings has been provided by the Austrian Cultural Forum New York.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Battle of Tuntenhaus
screenings.description: Juliet BashoreTHE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 1 1991, 24 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.THE BATTLE OF TUNTENHAUS, PART 2 1992, 19 min, DCP. In German with English subtitles.“The Wall has fallen. Berlin has reunified. But there are new zones of transgression to be carved out and explored. Mainzer Straße is a hot spot of squatters and anti-fascist fights. One of the squats on this notorious street, the Tuntenhaus (‘House of Queers’), becomes a specific target of both their neo-Nazi neighbors and the iron fist of the capitalist state. Juliet Bashore’s legendary documentary follows the daily struggle of the queens and queers to create and defend a place for themselves in the chaos and unrest after the fall of communism. The extraordinary union of the anarchist/autonomous and gay scenes meets the onlooking yet involved sympathizers, who also end up in conflict with the squatters as a result of their filming. The film is a unique testimony to the violent and momentous eviction of the people from the streets.” –THE BEACONCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Einsturzende Neubauten: Liebeslieder
screenings.description: An essential text for anyone with a love for the avant-garde. The explosive soundscapes of industrial music titans Einstürzende Neubauten first shook Berlin – then the whole world – to its core in the 1980s. In LIEBESLIEDER, co-directors Klaus Maeck and Johanna Schenkel wield a fractured feast of killer Neubauten performances from Euro television: ones that highlight the group’s cinematic presence, wild handmade instruments, and totally unique style. For those who are at all curious about industrial or noise music in general, this sweaty documentary is unmissable. For Neubauten fans, this humanizing portrait of their first decade provides a fresh take on the band.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bitter Christmas
screenings.description: BITTER CHRISTMAS tells two alternating stories, one starring Elsa, an advertising director, in 2004, during a long weekend in December. The second takes place in 2026 and stars Raúl, a screenwriter and director who is writing a script that we soon discover is the story of Elsa, her boyfriend Bonifacio, and her friends Patricia and Natalia. Mixed with fiction, Elsa is, in a way, Raúl's alter ego, who, like him, resorts to autofiction as a solution to a long period of creative drought. He looks inside himself, and he can't help but also look at the people who make up his most intimate universe: his partner and his assistant. The film narrates the close relationship between reality and fiction, between inspiration and life, exploring the limits of autofiction and stories within stories.

screenings.title: Postcolonial Motion: Taxis and Travelogues
screenings.description: While not as long-standing as the romance with trains, cinema has a love affair with taxis. A cab ride is often more than just a means of getting from one place to another. The taxi is a cinematic apparatus in motion, a confessional, an urban microcosm, a transition, a temporary intimacy, an archive of daily life, a nightmare of forced conversation, an eavesdropper’s dream. Yet beneath such metaphors are material threats: the gig economy, prior and enduring precarities and exploitation of labor, movements of migration conditioned by colonization.POSTCOLONIAL MOTION: TAXIS AND TRAVELOGUES draws together three films combining oral testimonies and the kinetics of transport. Frank Sweeney, Karimah Ashadu, and Timoteus Anggawan Kusno each consider the movements of people, goods and images, tracing how workers warp the barriers of historical categories and economic constraints as they cross borders.Guest-programmed by Yasmina Price, who wrote the introduction and individual film descriptions.Frank SweeneyGO YE AFAR2026, 24 min, DCPIrish research-based artist Frank Sweeney’s latest work, GO YE AFAR (2026), stages a historical examination of economy, religion, national identity, and state power through the nocturnal taxi journey of a Nigerian driver in Dublin and Calabar. Making a link between the IMF’s role in imposing a debt structure on Ireland in the 2010s and the economic dependency still inflicted on the African continent, Sweeney makes a taxi journey an illuminating lens onto the dubious legacies of Catholic missionaries and European philanthropy, global privatization and the erosion of the commons.Karimah AshaduBROWN GOODS2020, 12 min, DCPBROWN GOODS (2020), by British-born Nigerian artist and director Karimah Ashadu, both shares and reconfigures a similar terrain. The film scans the intermingled economies and geographies of Africa and Europe, conjuring Nigeria from its viewpoint in Germany. The setting is specifically Hamburg, a hub of international trade and multinational corporations. Ashadu’s agile camerawork delves through docks, weaving amongst ship containers and stacks of tires as Emeka – the self-sufficient central figure, excluded from formal work due to his humanitarian status – voices a sharp analysis of manufacturing and industrial monopolies, the politics of resources and global capital.Timoteus Anggawan KusnoOBSCURA2026, 14 min, DCPIndonesian filmmaker and visual artist Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s OBSCURA (2026) echoes the unsettling, spectral dreaminess and mediatized archival memory of GO YE AFAR. Operating between Indonesia and the Netherlands, the film critically reworks the form of the ethnographic travelogue and colonial imagery through a story of theft (another kind of informal job). Gallery workers liberate a painting and carry it out in a truck, performing how images physically travel, are taken apart, literally unframed and reframed.Total running time: ca. 55 min.The screening will be followed by a conversation with filmmaker and artist Frank Sweeney!CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Drunken Noodles
screenings.description: Lucio CastroDRUNKEN NOODLES2025, 83 min, DCP. In English and Spanish with English subtitles.When Adnan (Laith Khalifeh) arrives in New York to work at a Lower East Side gallery for the summer, he’s newly single and ready to mingle. He cruises strangers in the park at night and begins a flirtation with a delivery driver. At work, he’s helping to exhibit the recently discovered work of Sal Salandra, a real-world gay artist and elder who crafts tableaus of gay orgies and sex club scenes in vibrant needlepoint. These artworks – and Sal himself, played by Ezriel Kornel – become the connective thread for a time-jumping narrative that unfolds in four parts. screenings.title: Barbara
screenings.description: With Jeanne Balibar, Mathieu Amalric, Vincent Peirani, Aurore Clement, and Grégoire Colin.Amalric’s seventh feature-length film as a director is both a heartfelt tribute to the legendary chanteuse Barbara (1930-97), and a vehicle for another peerlessly talented French luminary, the actress and singer Jeanne Balibar. Amalric’s films are remarkable for their intuitive freedom, and their emphasis on emotional textures and states of feeling rather than on straightforward narrative construction or easily grasped meanings. BARBARA is a case in point: eschewing anything like a coherent, birth-to-death account of the events of her life, the film instead orchestrates fragments of the singer’s life and performances into a free and quasi-abstract meditation on Barbara’s identity and cultural presence. And by casting Balibar not as Barbara per se but more self-referentially as an actress making a film-within-the-film about the singer, his film becomes an even broader investigation into the concept of biographical filmmaking, representation, and identity. An experimental biopic in the tradition of Stanley Kwan’s CENTER STAGE, Peter Watkins’s EDVARD MUNCH, and Paul Leduc’s FRIDA, it features a typically riveting, charismatic performance from Balibar.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Cabaret
screenings.description: Dir. Bob Fosse. 1972, 124 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Liza Minnelli, Michael York, Helmut Griem, Joel Grey, Maria Berenson. Fosse rightly won the Best Director Oscar for his shattering musical set in Berlin on the eve of Hitler’s rise to power. Liza Minnelli and Joel Grey also scored Oscars for their unforgettable performances as, respectively, Sally Bowles, a vivacious but damaged American singer selling her soul in a seedy nightclub, and the devilish emcee who presides over it. A devastating, delirious movie experience, featuring John Kander and Fred Ebb’s rousing show tunes and Geoffrey Unsworth’s gloriously ragged photography, Cabaret reinvented the movie musical for 1970s American cinema and all but wrote a new cinematic grammar for how to shoot and edit song and dance. Minnelli’s phenomenally directed and acted tale of rootlessness in post–World War II America stars Frank Sinatra as a war veteran and former writer who has fallen into alcoholism, and who returns to his Indiana hometown to find nothing is quite as he remembered it. screenings.title: 16mm Cartoons: Raunchy, Sexy & Risqué + Q&A
screenings.description: Back in the ‘pre-code’ era of the 1920s and early 1930s, animated cartoons were made to entertain the adults in the audience. The results were often sexually suggestive, if not borderline explicit. Much later, with the long overdue relaxation of old censorship codes, independent and experimental animators of the 1960s and beyond became free to openly explore the raunchy and risqué once more. Salacious sexiness, lustful adultery, queerness, Peeping Toms, and other questionable—or perfectly human—adult behaviors were only some of the wonderfully ‘vulgar’ themes present in animated shorts made in both eras.

screenings.title: Leave Her to Heaven

Shot in gorgeous technicolor by director John M. Stahl and DP Leon Shamroy (winner of the Academy Award for Best Color Cinematography), Leave Her to Heaven became 20th Century Fox’s highest-grossing film of the 1940’s. At the rotten center is an Oscar-nominated performance from Tierney, playing the rare femme fatale who isn’t motivated by all-American greed and ambition, but instead is consumed by obsession, jealousy, and deadly devotion.

screenings.title: Ec: Intolerance
screenings.description: Griffith’s immensely influential silent epic intercuts four parallel tales from history (spanning Babylon, Christ’s Judea, Reformation Europe, and turn-of-the-century America) to embroider a moral tapestry on personal, social, and political repression through the ages. The visual poetry is overwhelming, especially in the massed crowd scenes, and the unbridled eroticism of the Babylon harem scenes demonstrates just what Hollywood lost when it later bowed to the Hays Code. While the (partly self-financed) production ruined Griffith financially and baffled audiences with its multiple plots and labyrinthine structure, it has been enormously influential on generations of filmmakers, including Eisenstein, who studied the film closely.CLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1964. 95 mins. 35mm. With Peter Sellers, George C. Scott, Sterling Hayden, Slim Pickens, Keenan Wynn. Stanley Kubrick reinvents the nuclear suspense thriller, then in vogue, as an absurdist black comedy in this brilliant evocation of cold war paranoia. Dr. Strangelove, co-written by Kubrick and Terry Southern, strikes just the right manic, irreverent, sexually charged tone, creating a satirical masterpiece that is one of the seminal counterculture works of the 1960s. Towering over the cast—which also includes George C. Scott as the blustering General Buck Turgidson and Sterling Hayden as “precious bodily fluids”–obsessed General Jack D. Ripper—is Sellers, a triple threat as meek RAF Captain Mandrake, bungling U.S. President Merkin Muffley, and, of course, the mad scientist title character—inventor of the doomsday machine that may wipe out humanity as we know it.
